title: Planar Focusing of Anisotropic Plasmon Polaritons in MoOCl2/Au
content:
Propagating Au SPPs are employed as a controllable excitation input, converted into hybrid anisotropic polaritons through momentum matching in a MoOCl2/Au heterostructure, and subsequently utilized for extended planar focusing. This two‐stage focusing enables simultaneous long‐distance propagation and strong spatial confinement, achieving a focal distance of 2.5λ and a focal spot of approximately λ/5 at 633 nm.








ABSTRACT
Hyperbolic polaritons offer a promising approach for subwavelength light confinement and manipulation. While extensively explored across mid‐infrared to terahertz bands, achieving long‐distance focusing at visible frequencies remains challenging due to the trade‐off between long propagation and strong compression. In this work, we demonstrate planar focusing of anisotropic plasmon polaritons with an extended focal length in a MoOCl2/Au heterostructure. By integrating an Au metastructure with the natural hyperbolic material MoOCl2, we convert surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) into surface plasmon hyperbolic polaritons (SPHPs), enabling excitation and focusing of the low‐momentum hybrid anisotropic polariton in the heterostructure. Furthermore, by optimizing the thickness of the MoOCl2 layer, we synergistically enhance both the propagation distance and the field compression. Using transmission‐mode scanning near‐field optical microscopy (SNOM) and quantitative methods, we demonstrate a focal length of 2.5λ and a focal spot with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of λ/5 under 633 nm excitation, accompanied by a threefold energy enhancement. This visible‐frequency long‐focus system offers significant potential for noncontact nanoscale probing, integrated photonics, and optical interconnects. The proposed heterostructure engineering approach provides a versatile design paradigm for coupling hyperbolic polaritons with multiple plasmonic excitations, paving the way for advanced photonic applications.

title: Hydro‐Gated Photonic Actuators With Programmable Color and Shape
content:
Hydro‐gated photonic actuators with programmable color and shape: This work presents a hydro‐switchable photonic liquid crystal network integrating scattering‐gated structural color switching with programmable actuation. In a dry state, interface scattering masks the structural color of the soft actuator, while water wetting makes the vivid structural color of the actuator appear and triggers its controllable deformation.








ABSTRACT
Structural color actuators integrating visual readout with motion are prized for biomimicry, yet typically operate in a coupled, color‐gradient mode with limited freedom. Here we report a photonic liquid crystal network that decouples these responses via a scattering‐gated mechanism. The material hides its structural color in the dry state but, upon water uptake, simultaneously switches on vivid coloration and executes programmable three‐dimensional deformation. Crucially, we achieve stimulus‐selective control: ethanol turns on color without motion, while heat induces motion without color. This independent, on‐demand manipulation of optical and mechanical outputs offers a transformative platform for multi‐responsive soft robotics, adaptive camouflage, and smart displays.

title: Engineering Topological Phases in Two‐Dimensional Materials: A Path from Preparation to Device Applications
content:
This review presents recent advances in phase engineering of two‐dimensional topological materials, emphasizing their classification, growth strategies, phase modulation techniques, and integration into electronic and spintronic devices. It highlights the transition from theoretical understanding to scalable fabrication, offering insights into challenges and opportunities for future device‐level applications.








ABSTRACT
Owing to their topologically protected edge or surface states, rapid electronic transport, and highly tunable physical properties, two‐dimensional topological materials (2D TMs) have garnered significant attention in condensed matter physics and materials science, and are regarded as potential candidates for quantum computing. Since the first observation of the quantum Hall effect, fundamental research on the physics of TMs has made remarkable progress. To better utilize the unique properties of TMs, the importance of material fabrication and phase engineering of topological states has become increasingly prominent. This review systematically discusses phase engineering in 2D TMs, from their growth to device applications. First, various topological phases and related 2D materials are introduced briefly. Next, the growth methods for 2D TMs are summarized. It then discusses progress and limitations in growth, driven by the requirements of characterization and application. Furthermore, the general approaches for modulating topological phases are reviewed, alongside the current applications in electronic devices. Finally, the review outlines future directions and challenges in phase engineering of 2D topological materials, aiming to promote the transition of 2D TMs from fundamental physics research to phase‐engineered material platforms.

title: Over 95% Optical Reflectance From Structurally Modulated All‐Biopolymer Multilayers
content:
A new dense–porous design turns ordinary polysaccharides into highly reflective photonic multilayers. Alternating dense pectin and porous cellulose nanofiber layers create strong refractive‐index contrast without inorganic or synthetic polymers, enabling nearly perfect visible reflection, high near‐infrared reflection, broadband metallic‐like colors, planar patterning, and transparent thermal‐management performance.








ABSTRACT
Sustainable photonics aims to replace conventional optical materials with environmentally benign alternatives, yet its development is fundamentally constrained by the narrow intrinsic refractive‐index variability of biopolymers. Here we show that a dense–porous periodic architecture yields nearly perfect optical reflection using only polysaccharides. By exploiting the difference in skeletal rigidity between amorphous pectin and crystalline cellulose nanofibers (CNFs), we form alternating dense, high‐refractive‐index pectin layers and porous, low‐refractive‐index CNF layers through a combination of electrodeposition with solvent exchange. This dense–porous periodic architecture yields reflectivities exceeding 97% in the visible range and 95% in the near‐infrared—a range unprecedented for biopolymer‐based optical materials. Moreover, the strategy is simple, scalable, and highly versatile, enabling free spectral design across the visible and near‐infrared regions, broadband metallic‐like reflection, and planar patterning within a single fabrication process. Combined with the low thermal conductivity arising from porous layers and the coexistence of visible transparency and near‐infrared reflection, the resulting films show potential as transparent thermal‐management materials. This work establishes a new materials design principle for biodegradable, polysaccharide‐based photonic systems and advances the field of sustainable photonics.

title: Ultra‐Long Helical CNFs 3D‐Networks as High‐Conductivity Current Collectors for Efficient Sodium Deposition
content:
High‐density NiY–DAC confined in the 20 nm Cu layer enables the catalytic fabrication of ultra‐long helical CNFs with a thickness of 46.3 µm as high‐conductivity current collectors. The CNFs‐Na||Na3V2(PO4)3 full cells achieve stable cycling over 1500 cycles at 10 C.








ABSTRACT
Aluminum (Al) current collectors are crucial for sodium metal batteries (SMBs), yet sodium (Na) dendrite suppression and uniform Na deposition remain challenges. Surface modification could significantly optimize Na deposition behavior. Herein, a 20 nm copper (Cu) layer is designed to confine NiY diatomic catalyst (DAC) for Al surface modification via magnetron sputtering and heat treatment. The adjacent NiY atoms, with low single‐point energy (–228.05 eV), minimum segregation energy (−0.67 eV), and maximum aggregation energy (5.84 eV), synergistically stabilize diatomic dispersion in the Cu nanolayer. Benefiting from the tailored acetylene adsorption energy (−1.16 eV) and favorable formation energies of C2H (−13.58 eV) and C2 (−11.44 eV), NiY–DAC exhibits excellent catalytic activity, in‐situ growth ultra‐long helical CNFs 3D‐networks with a thickness of 46.3 µm on Al current collectors, enabling efficient Na storage and remarkable inhibition Na dendrite formation. The modified current collector delivers outstanding electrochemical performance. The coulombic efficiency is up to 99.49% over 3000 h of half‐cells at 1.0 mA cm−2/1.0 mAh cm−2 with a low overpotential (3.1 mV), and the CNFs‐Na||Na3V2(PO4)3 full‐cells achieve stable cycling over 1500 cycles at 10.0 C. This diatomic catalyst confinement strategy provides new insight into designing high‐performance carbon‐modified current collectors.

title: Flexible High‐Speed Low‐Noise Organic Photodiode Arrays for Dynamic Near‐Infrared Imaging
content:
An organic photonic imaging system leverages stabilized phase separation and enhanced thermodynamic stability to deliver high responsivity, low dark current, and rapid photoresponse. These superior optoelectronic properties enable reliable motion detection and high‐fidelity dynamic image reconstruction, offering a promising platform for real‐time motion tracking and next‐generation intelligent optoelectronic imaging applications.








ABSTRACT
Organic photodiodes (OPDs) hold significant promise for next‐generation IoT optical sensing and low‐power imaging applications. However, widespread application of OPD in flexible and dynamic imaging has been constrained by high dark current, poor stability, and the lack of a cost‐effective imaging system. In this work, we present an integrated solution through tailoring pseudo‐planar heterojunction (PPHJ) OPD arrays and a customized, rapidly accessible imaging system, the dynamic organic photonics imaging system (DOIS). The resulting PPHJ OPD exhibited a high responsivity (0.6 A W−1 at 868 nm), low dark current (1.5 × 10−8 A cm−2 at −1 V) and fast response time (480 ns), benefiting from optimal vertical phase separation and donor‐acceptor interface morphology. Moreover, flexible photodetector exhibits superior mechanical stability, photostability and storage stability. Crucially, a pixel‐shifting strategy was incorporated into conventional convolutional neural network (CNN) based machine learning algorithms to capture dynamic images and enhance resolution by leveraging sub‐pixel information sampling. This work demonstrates a significant potential for the extensive application of organic photovoltaic materials in image sensing and flexible electronics.

title: Crystallinity‐Governed Liquid Wettability and Mobility on Solid Surface
content:
Modulation of molecular packing in the selected semicrystalline homopolymer regulates liquid droplet wettability and slippery property. Unlike permanent chemical modifications, current approach relies on the spatially selective difference in crystalline packing to design a reversible, reconfigurable, and patterned wettability for guided liquid manipulation across diverse surface tensions. Such patterns further enable microdroplet arrays, providing reconfigurable platforms for customized microliter‐scale chemical reactions.








ABSTRACT
Control over liquid wettability and droplet mobility is essential for several emerging applications including open microfluidics, anti‐icing, self‐cleaning, and heat transfer. Existing strategies generally rely on permanent chemical modification or continuous external stimuli to regulate droplet spreading, pinning, and sliding. Here, we report a unified approach for reconfiguring wettability states and droplet mobility by regulating crystalline packing of a semicrystalline polymer. A phase‐transitioning polymer, poly(octadecyl acrylate) (PODAc), was incorporated into a porous polymeric coating, where melting and subsequent cooling pathways determine the extent of alkyl‐chain crystallization and interfacial polar functionality. Cooling in air or underwater generates reversibly switchable hydrophilic (θW ∼ 85°), hydrophobic (θW ∼ 104°), and amphiphobic slippery states across liquids with surface tensions of 22–72 mN m−1. These distinct regimes enable programmable droplet spreading, pinning, and low‐friction transport without post‐synthetic chemical treatment or sustained external stimulation. Furthermore, reconfigurable wettability patterns enable guided liquid transport through spatially selective complete wetting or customized contact line frictional force.

title: Additives and Relaxation Fluidize Molecular Transport Within Covalent Adaptable Networks
content:
A photo‐releasable catalyst reveals how formulation and dynamic covalent exchange independently regulate molecular transport in crosslinked networks. Photobase incorporation produces the dominant reduction in trapping and spatial heterogeneity, while catalyst release enables a smaller, distinct post‐cure enhancement. Single‐molecule tracking exposes how additives and bond exchange reshape nanoscale diffusion beyond bulk mechanical behavior.








ABSTRACT
Incorporating dynamic covalent bonds into polymer networks could offer stimuli‐responsive control over molecular transport, often requiring additives to facilitate bond rearrangement. Here super‐resolution localization microscopy was employed to examine fluorescent probe transport in unhydrated, elastic networks containing thiol‐thioester dynamic covalent chemistry (DCC). In static, DCC‐free networks, displacement distributions revealed frequent trapping and slow, anomalous, and heterogeneous diffusion. Introducing a dynamic catalyst additive markedly increased mobile fraction and produced diffusivity that was more fluid‐like. These effects were observed with several classes of fluorescent probes, two distinct additives, and for networks with or without DCC. Experiments with a photo‐releasable catalyst (NPPOC‐TMG) separated additive effects from those of activated exchange. Catalyst release conferred additional fluidization of the network. Importantly, these changes were not accompanied by macroscopic plasticization, suggesting that small additive concentrations can strongly affect transport in confining environments. Spatial analysis further indicated that transport enhancement was primarily due to restructuring of an initially heterogeneous network rather than local bond exchange near the diffusing probes. Additive incorporation and post‐cure exchange likely reduced defects and homogenized the crosslink density. In sum, these results demonstrate how DCC modulates transport, emphasize the importance of the activation method, and highlight its potential in separation and controlled‐release systems.

title: Ultra‐Broad‐Temperature Mechanoluminescence Enabled by Intrinsic Lattice Disorder
content:
Intrinsic lattice disorder creates a quasi‐continuous trap landscape, enabling trap‐relay‐mediated carrier redistribution and stable mechanoluminescence over an ultrabroad temperature range of 133–433 K. This work establishes a strategy for thermally robust luminescent materials for extreme‐environment applications.








ABSTRACT
Mechanoluminescent (ML) materials convert mechanical stimuli into light through carrier excitation and radiative recombination, enabling external‐power‐free stress sensing and visualization. The strict energy matching required for carrier release, transport, and recombination restricts ML to narrow thermal windows. Their application at extreme temperatures, however, is constrained by discrete defect levels arising from relatively uniform local atomic environments. Here, we use intrinsic lattice disorder to engineer a quasi‐continuous trap landscape in Sr3Gd2(Ge3O9)2:Mn2+. Diverse local crystal‐field environments, together with dynamically generated defects, create energetically adjacent traps that support a trap‐relay process. Charge carriers are continuously redistributed across this trap manifold, sustaining stable ML over an ultrabroad temperature range from 133 to 433 K. We further demonstrate a human‐machine interaction system based on this material under simulated extreme‐temperature conditions. These results establish intrinsic lattice disorder as a strategy for broadening the thermal operating window of ML materials and provide a general design principle for thermally robust, energy‐storing luminescent materials for extreme environments.

title: Sulfur Locking and Chlorination Synergistically Enable Efficient Charge Transport and Low Nonradiative Energy Loss in Organic Solar Cells
content:
Sulfur locking and chlorination establish an effective strategy for balancing charge transport and nonradiative energy loss in organic solar cells. Enhanced intermolecular packing promotes exciton diffusion and carrier transport, while intrinsically low reorganization energy and weak electron–phonon coupling suppress nonradiative recombination, enabling 20.0% binary and 21.3% ternary device efficiencies.








ABSTRACT
Achieving efficient charge transport while maintaining low nonradiative energy loss remains a key challenge in the molecular design of small‐molecule acceptors (SMAs) for organic solar cells (OSCs). Herein, we report a stepwise molecular engineering strategy based on sulfur locking and chlorination to regulate intermolecular packing and excited‐state properties simultaneously. Sulfur locking modifies molecular conformation and intermolecular packing, leading to enhanced exciton diffusion and charge transport. Subsequent chlorination further strengthens intermolecular interactions through additional Cl···S contacts, resulting in tighter π–π stacking and improved crystalline ordering. Binary OSCs based on D18:Qx2Ph‐SCl achieve an efficiency of 20.0% with a high open‐circuit voltage (VOC) of 0.951 V, while maintaining a low nonradiative energy loss of ∼0.19 eV. Owing to its intrinsically lower reorganization energy and weaker electron–phonon coupling than L8‐BO, Qx2Ph‐SCl further serves as an effective third component in ternary OSCs, reducing nonradiative recombination and increasing the VOC. As a result, the ternary device delivers an efficiency of 21.3%. This work demonstrates that stepwise sulfur locking and chlorination provide an effective molecular design strategy for simultaneously optimizing charge transport and voltage loss in high‐performance OSCs.

title: PASS‐Derived O/S Donor Field‐Directed Competitive–Cooperative Fe/Co Phase Evolution for Cross‐Band Microwave Absorption
content:
A PASS‐derived O/S heterogeneous donor field amplifies the non‐equivalent coordination responses of Fe and Co, directing competitive‐cooperative nonequilibrium phase evolution and the coupled formation of multiphase interfaces, defects, and local strain. The resulting structural and electronic reconstruction redistributes magnetic‐dielectric loss channels, enabling efficient cross‐band microwave absorption.








ABSTRACT
Fe/Co bimetallic regulation enables high‐performance microwave absorbers, yet the role of intrinsic coordination disparity in precursor conversion, nonequilibrium phase evolution, and cross‐band loss redistribution remains unclear. We design a poly(arylene sulfide sulfone) (PASS)‐predefined O/S heterogeneous donor‐field strategy to direct competitive–cooperative nonequilibrium phase evolution in Fe/Co systems. Covalently embedded sulfone‐O and thioether‐S sites, with PASS's rigid backbone, create a molecularly preorganized donor field that amplifies non‐equivalent Fe/Co coordination, promoting competitive bonding, differentiated phase pathways, and electronic‐state reconstruction during confined pyrolysis. Fe/Co regulation thus reshapes local phases, O/S chemical environments, and interfacial charge states via Fe─O/Co─S coordination preferences, generating multiphase heterostructures, amorphous/crystalline interfaces, defects, and lattice strain while balancing dielectric polarization, conductive transport, magnetic response, and impedance matching. The resulting CFC absorber achieves cross‐band absorption in low‐frequency 5G and high‐frequency radar bands. CFC‐4 exhibits −73.83 dB at 6.23 GHz (3.20 mm) and −76.59 dB at 16.98 GHz (1.31 mm), with a maximum EAB of 5.03 GHz. CFC‐4∼6 (1–5 mm) show >90% cumulative effective absorption over 2–18 GHz. Finite‐element simulations reveal a maximum RCS reduction of 42.5 dB on PEC. This work establishes O/S donor‐field engineering as a viable route to amplify Fe/Co coordination differentiation for efficient cross‐band microwave absorption.

title: Scalable Gigapascal Strength Bamboo Veneers via Nanocellulose Reinforcement
content:
This study reports a new class of bamboo derived structural fibers with high mechanical performance and low carbon emissions. A nanocellulose reinforcement strategy reprograms bamboo cell walls through CNC infiltration and densification, enabling reinforced bamboo veneers with a tensile strength of 0.98 GPa and a modulus of 52.7 GPa. This scalable approach provides a sustainable alternative to carbon intensive structural materials.








ABSTRACT
Carbon neutrality demands materials that deliver both performance and low environmental impact. Carbon fiber and glass fiber rely on fossil feedstocks and energy‐intensive processing, while nature bamboo the ecological marvel is limited by inefficient load transfer within their heterogeneous cell walls. Here we show that this limitation can be overcome by reprogramming the bamboo cell wall through supramolecular nano‐reinforcement. Cellulose nanocrystals infiltrate the cell wall and promote the reorganization of the interfacial hydrogen‐bonding network within the aligned cellulose framework converting structural discontinuities into a continuous load‐bearing scaffold. This enhances interfibrillar stress transfer and homogenizes mechanical response across scales. The resulting material achieves a tensile strength of 0.98 GPa and a Young's modulus of 52.7 GPa, with specific strength rivaling many synthetic fiber materials. These gains are achieved with up to two orders of magnitude lower carbon intensity than that of carbon fiber. This work demonstrates a scalable route to transform abundant biomass into high‐performance structural materials, decoupling mechanical performance from carbon intensity.

title: Porphyrin Integration Enhances Bipolar Redox Accessibility for High‐Rate Sodium‐Based Dual‐Ion Storage
content:
Integrating porphyrin into a sulfur‐rich benzotrithiophene–thiophene conjugated polymer creates a chemically diversified redox framework for sodium dual‐ion storage. Compared with the reference polymer BTB, porphyrin‐integrated BTTP enables complementary anion/cation compensation by regulating local electronic environments, thereby enhancing the accessibility of intrinsic multielectron redox chemistry.








ABSTRACT
Closing the gap between theoretical multielectron capacity and practical accessibility remains the central bottleneck for high‐energy organic batteries. Herein, we report a molecular design strategy that integrates a porphyrin motif into a sulfur‐rich conjugated polymer (BTTP) to align electronic structure, state‐dependent ion interactions, and electrochemical kinetics across the bipolar window. Despite possessing a lower theoretical capacity than its reference counterpart (BTB), BTTP achieves an exceptional theoretical capacity utilization of 94.2% (delivering 477 mAh g−1 at 0.5 A g−1, compared to only 53.5% and 351 mAh g−1 for BTB). Electrokinetic analyses, including GITT and DRT, confirm accelerated apparent ion diffusion and reduced polarization limitations, enabling BTTP to retain 166 mAh g−1 at an ultrahigh current density of 20 A g−1 over 25 000 cycles. Operando/ex situ spectroscopy and theoretical calculations elucidate that the dual pyrrolic/imino nitrogen sites in porphyrin and the sulfur‐rich backbone cooperatively provide potential‐dependent coordination environments for PF6− anions and Na+ cations. This work suggests that molecular regulation of complementary ion‐interaction environments within multi‐active‐unit frameworks, rather than simply increasing the number of redox units, is important for enhancing rate capability and capacity utilization.

title: Boron‐Oxygen Covalent Fusion Enables Narrowband Deep‐Red CP‐OLEDs Based on BODIPY Emitters
content:
Boron–oxygen covalent fusion enables the first solution‐processed narrowband deep‐red circularly polarized hyperfluorescence organic light‐emitting diodes, delivering a 34 nm full width at half maximum, a |gEL| up to 5.49 × 10−3 and CIE coordinates approaching the NTSC red standard. 








ABSTRACT
Realizing solution‐processable deep‐red circularly polarized organic light‐emitting diodes (CP‐OLEDs) with both intense CP and high color purity remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report the first solution‐processed narrowband deep‐red circularly polarized hyperfluorescence OLEDs based on a helically chiral boron‐dipyrromethene emitter. Intramolecular boron–oxygen (B–O) covalent fusion simultaneously regulates molecular conjugation and conformational rigidity, thereby suppressing excited‐state structural relaxation and vibronic coupling while preserving efficient deep‐red emission. As a result, BDP‐BO exhibits deep‐red emission at 654 nm with a high photoluminescence quantum yield of 71% and an ultranarrow emission bandwidth of 34 nm (0.10 eV). The corresponding P‐ and M‐enantiomers display excellent chiroptical activity, with a luminescence dissymmetry factor (|glum|) up to 3.54 × 10−3 and a circularly polarized luminescence brightness (BCPL) of 49 M−1 cm−1. Exploiting these merits, the M‐BDP‐BO‐based device delivers deep‐red electroluminescence (EL) within the National Television System Committee color gamut, a maximum external quantum efficiency of 2.6%, and a large EL dissymmetry factor (|gEL|) of 5.49 × 10−3. This work establishes B–O covalent fusion as an effective strategy for simultaneously regulating molecular conjugation and conformational rigidity, providing a versatile platform for high‐performance solution‐processed deep‐red CP‐OLEDs.

title: π‐Extended Bisallyls Through Valence Isomerism: From Transient Diradicals to Persistent Anions
content:
π‐Extension brings the hidden bisallyl intermediates of allene dimerization within thermal reach. NMR exchange and calculations identify transient open‐shell singlet diradicals, while reduction reverses the valence‐isomer preference and stabilizes persistent ring‐opened anions through charge‐controlled covalent‐bond reorganization.








ABSTRACT
Bisallyl diradicals are central intermediates in allene dimerization, yet they are normally too short‐lived to observe under thermal conditions. Here, π‐extension of Staudinger‐type allene dimers weakens the central cyclobutane bond sufficiently to make reversible ring opening accessible near room temperature. Variable‐temperature NMR spectroscopy and ROESY exchange correlations reveal repeated cleavage and reformation of this bond, with activation free energies of 15.77 and 13.79 kcal mol−1 for the Staudinger dimer and its π‐expanded analogue, respectively. Calculations reproduce this trend and identify low‐population open‐shell singlet bisallyls as the intermediates, while explaining the absence of neutral‐state EPR signals. Reduction reverses the relative stability of the closed and open valence isomers. Voltammetry and chemical reduction support a sequence of ring‐opened radical‐anion, dianion, and tetraanion states. The dianion is characterized by NMR spectroscopy and x‐ray diffraction, while spectroscopy and calculations reveal progressive bond redistribution from mixed‐valence allyl‐radical/allyl‐anion character to two allyl‐anion units and, finally, four fluorenyl‐anion‐like termini. These results connect hidden neutral diradicals with persistent reduced bisallyl frameworks through charge‐controlled covalent‐bond reorganization.

title: Fluorinated Fullerene Derivatives for Thermally Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
A new type of fluorinated phenyl fullerene derivatives, FPCPB and 5FPCPB, were designed to reduce the self‐aggregation of phenyl‐C61‐butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM). Intermolecular interactions and steric hindrance can improve the microscopic aggregation of fullerenes, enhance the uniformity and stability of the electron transport layer (ETL), and strengthen electron transport. The optimized devices achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.42%, with excellent stability under continuous illumination and high‐temperature operation. 








ABSTRACT
PCBM (phenyl‐C61‐butyric acid methyl ester) is one of the most used electron transport layers (ETLs) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs). However, PCBM tends to self‐aggregate during the thermal aging process, disrupting film continuity and limiting device lifetime. To address this issue, we synthesized new fluorinated phenyl fullerene derivatives, FPCPB and 5FPCPB, forming a composite fullerene ETL by blending with PCBM. We found that fullerene self‐aggregation was suppressed through the synergistic effects of weak interactions, such as π–π conjugation between phenyl and fluorophenyl groups and C─H···F van der Waals interactions, and the constrained molecular conformation induced by intermolecular steric hindrance, thereby markedly improving film uniformity and thermal stability, reducing defect‐state density, and suppressing ion migration. In addition, the energy level alignment between perovskite and ETL is optimized, enhancing electron transport. Ultimately, 5FPCPB, having more compatible energy levels and stronger conjugation effects than FPCPB, achieved a 26.42% power conversion efficiency (PCE), with improved operational and thermal stability (T90 under light = 1200 h; T95 under 85°C > 700 h). The fullerene co‐doping strategy opens a new pathway for achieving high‐performance and thermally stable perovskite devices.

title: Mechanistic Insights Into the Solid‐State Redox Reactions: Role of Organic Piezoelectric Materials
content:
Crystal symmetry powers chemistry: Non‐centrosymmetric organic piezoelectric crystals convert mechanical energy into electrical polarization, enabling solid‐state redox reactions under ball milling. In contrast, chemically identical centrosymmetric crystal forms remain largely inactive. This symmetry‐dependent reactivity enables C─B, C─S, C─Se, C─C, and C─P bonds formation, establishing crystal symmetry as a powerful design principle for sustainable mechanochemical synthesis.








ABSTRACT
Mechanochemistry has gained tremendous recent attention because it combines sustainability with the ability to access unique reaction pathways and materials while offering practical advantages for efficient and scalable chemical synthesis. However, predicting solid‐state transformations from mechanical energy remains a formidable challenge, as the current mechanistic models are insufficient. While solid‐state electrocatalytic reactions in the presence of inorganic piezoelectric materials have been demonstrated recently, the ability of piezoelectric organic solids, which possess an order of magnitude lower piezoelectric coefficients, remain completely unexplored. Here, using different crystalline forms, we demonstrate that under ball‐milling, non‐centrosymmetric organic crystals generate piezoelectric potentials that are sufficient to drive a range of redox bond‐forming reactions, including C─B, C─S, C─Se, C─C, and C─P couplings. To further evaluate the role of piezoelectricity, we compared chemically identical crystal forms of a compound, differing only in symmetry: Non‐centrosymmetric crystals are highly reactive, whereas centrosymmetric counterparts remain largely inert. These findings reveal crystal symmetry as a previously unrecognized determinant of chemical function and identify organic piezoelectric solids as active energy‐transduction media for chemical synthesis. More broadly, this work provides a framework for designing self‐powered chemical systems that directly couple mechanical energy harvesting with molecular transformation.

title: Guest Transition Metals in Host Keplerate Nanocapsules as Supramolecular Inorganic Functional Mimics of Monooxygenase Enzymes
content:
A Keplerate, an inorganic, porous buckyball was used as a host for copper metal cations ligated by histidine surrogates. Prepared by a simple assembly technique, the guest–host complex was used as a primitive biomimetic model of a monooxygenase enzyme complex, where C─H bonds were electrocatalytically hydroxylated by oxygen under reducing conditions. The confined space at the catalytic site yielded rate accelerations of two‐orders of magnitude.








ABSTRACT
Advanced design of supramolecules can mimic enzyme complexes. Methane monooxygenases have several subparts, hydroxylases active for alkane oxidation, and complexes and channels that regulate electron, proton, substrate, and product access to the active site. The replication of a hydroxylase active site with inclusion of regulatory functionalities within a porous Keplerate nanocapsule host was undertaken. A Cu active site guest within a Keplerate cavity was prepared by an assembly reaction using a histidine surrogate as binding site for CuII. The guest–host assembly enables transfer of protons and electrons and enables substrate and product diffusion to and from an active site into confined space. Characterization of the guest–host complex was by NMR, XPS, infrared, and Raman spectroscopies. Cyclic voltammetry was used to identify possible hydroxylase reactivity, followed by controlled potential electrolysis to verify hydrocarbon oxygenation. Substrate scope, optimal cathodic potential, and the number of metal sites needed were surveyed. Comparison of substrate reactivity revealed that their access to the active site was rate determining. Kinetics of a “dummy” substrate and product diffusion was measured by Guest Exchange Saturation Transfer 19F NMR. These guest–host Keplerate nanocapsules represent an initial foray into the mimicking of a complicated metalloenzyme complex in an inorganic synthetic system.

title: Oxidative‐Branch Engineering for Radical Regulation in Methane‐to‐Methanol Photocatalysis
content:
Selective methane‐to‐methanol photocatalysis requires a radical environment that activates methane while suppressing methanol overoxidation. Engineering the oxidative ZnO branch of an In2O3/ZnO S‐scheme heterojunction regulates this environment, delivering methanol at 638.2 µmol g−1 h−1 with 93.8% selectivity. Methanol selectivity is governed by a kinetic balance between productive oxidation and overoxidation, rather than by radical maximization.








ABSTRACT
Selective methane‐to‐methanol photocatalysis requires efficient methane activation and control over the radical environment that determines whether methanol is preserved or further oxidized. Radical generation is therefore double‐edged: an underdeveloped radical environment limits C–H activation and methanol‐forming oxygenation, whereas an excessive oxidative environment promotes secondary oxidation. Here, the radical environment is regulated by engineering the oxidative branch of an In2O3/ZnO S‐scheme heterojunction. Under ambient‐pressure gas–solid flow conditions with O2 and H2O as co‐reactants, the optimized catalyst delivers methanol at 638.2 µmol g−1 h−1 with 93.8% selectivity. The volcano‐shaped dependence of methanol productivity on ZnO loading shows that methanol accumulation is governed by competition between partial and deep oxidation rather than oxidative strength alone. Spectroscopic analyses support an S‐scheme charge‐transfer pathway that preserves oxidative holes on ZnO and reductive electrons on In2O3, coupling methane activation, water oxidation and O2 reduction within a branch‐specific redox network. Increasing ZnO loading strengthens the methyl‐, superoxide‐ and hydroxyl‐radical probe responses, whereas methanol selectivity peaks at an intermediate loading. At higher ZnO loading, deep‐oxidation signatures emerge without further enhancement of methanol‐related surface chemistry, whereas the optimized heterojunction maintains a formation‐dominant surface pathway. These findings identify a kinetic balance in the radical environment, rather than radical maximization, as the selectivity principle for methane‐to‐methanol photocatalysis.

title: An Ether‐Chain‐Functionalized Zwitterion Enables Mild Zinc‐Ion Coordination and Dual‐Site Polyiodide Capture in Aqueous Zinc–Iodine Batteries
content:
An ether‐chain‐functionalized zwitterion couples mild Zn2+ coordination with reversible dual‐site polyiodide capture. Imidazolium‐induced electrostatic repulsion facilitates Zn2+ dissociation and uniform deposition, while complementary electrostatic and ion–dipole interactions suppress polyiodide shuttling, enabling Zn–I2 cells to sustain >35 000 cycles and 300 mAh pouch cells to operate stably for >1200 cycles. 








ABSTRACT
Aqueous zinc–iodine batteries are limited by zinc dendrite growth at the anode and polyiodide shuttling at the cathode. Conventional strongly coordinating additives can regulate Zn2+ solvation, but the resulting high ligand‐dissociation barrier impedes interfacial charge transfer, creating an inherent trade‐off between solvation regulation and reaction kinetics. Here, we introduce ZEG, an ether‐chain‐functionalized imidazolium sulfonate zwitterion that combines mild Zn2+ coordination with dual‐site polyiodide capture. In ZEG, the imidazolium cation reduces the donor strength of the ether oxygens through electron‐withdrawing and further weakens ether‐chain coordination by electrostatically repelling Zn2+, thereby lowering the ligand‐dissociation barrier while preserving solvation‐shell regulation. Meanwhile, at the iodine cathode, the imidazolium cation and ether chain provide complementary sites that reversibly capture polyiodides through electrostatic attraction and ion–dipole interactions, respectively, thereby suppressing polyiodide shuttling and improving iodine utilization. With ZEG, Zn–I2 full cells sustain over 35,000 cycles at 10 A g−1, while 300 mAh pouch cells with a high iodine loading of 30 mg cm−2 operate stably for over 1200 cycles. By integrating mild Zn2+ coordination with reversible dual‐site polyiodide capture, this design reconciles solvation regulation with rapid interfacial charge transfer and offers an innovative molecular design principle for multifunctional electrolyte additives.

title: Chalcogen‐Bridge‐Regulated Proton Shuttling in Tantalum‐Doped Ruthenium Oxide for Robust Acidic Water Oxidation
content:
The in‐situ Raman spectroscopy, XRD, XPS, x‐ray absorption near edge structure (XANES), and pH‐dependent electrochemical tests support the bridge atoms in Ta─X─RuO2 strongly affect the proton shuttle during acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER). 








ABSTRACT
The acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) kinetics on ruthenium dioxide (RuO2) is fundamentally restricted by sluggish deprotonation and interfacial proton transfer. Herein, we introduce chalcogen atoms to tantalum doped RuO2 (Ta─X─RuO2, X = O, S, Se, and Te) and reveal its effects on proton shuttling, including deprotonation and proton transfer from electrocatalyst surface to bulk electrolyte. Significantly, Ta─S─RuO2 exhibits optimized OER performance due to the balanced hydrogen binding strength of bridge sulfur atoms, promoting deprotonation kinetics and modulating the interfacial water structure to form flexible hydrogen bond network for accelerated proton transfer. Only 1.89 V is demanded for Ta─S─RuO2 to reach 3 A cm−2geo and maintains robust performance for 1000 h with voltage decay of 49.0 µV h−1 stemming from the efficient hydrogen bond network to lower the local H+ concentration, suppressing the overoxidation of Ru. This work not only reports a novel high‐performance Ta─X─RuO2 electrocatalysts for acidic OER but also provides new insight into chalcogen‐regulated proton shuttling and promoted OER kinetics and stability, offering guidance to the design of future generation RuO2‐based electrocatalyst.

title: Transformer‐Guided Co‐Optimization of Mutation Prioritization and Thermodynamic Probe Design for Mutation Detection
content:
An iterative computational panel design framework in which biological mutation relevance and chemical probe discriminability are jointly optimized. Mutation attribution and population frequency prioritize biologically relevant targets, while MUT/WT binding free‐energy differences (ΔΔG°) guide probe design. The resulting 8‐plex assay enables sensitive mutation enrichment and detection down to 0.03% VAF.








ABSTRACT
The design of sequence‐selective DNA probes has long been limited by a decoupled workflow in which target selection proceeds without considering the physicochemical determinants of probe performance, such as thermodynamic stability and mismatch discrimination. Here, we establish an iterative computational design strategy that unifies mutation prioritization with chemical probe design. A custom transformer model extracts diagnostic attribution scores of mutations from 1,782 samples, generating semantic maps to guide probe placement. Candidate designs undergo in silico thermodynamic screening based on differential binding free energy. Probes failing to satisfy the integrated criteria of thermodynamic discrimination, diagnostic attribution, and population frequency are further evaluated by refining their spatial configuration to co‐optimize thermodynamic discriminability and clinical relevance. This iterative process converges on an 8‐plex targeted panel. Wet laboratory validation confirms 0.03% variant allele frequency detection with low assay cost and short turnaround time. Clinical testing on 375 samples achieves AUROC values of 0.96 for tissue and 0.90 for plasma. This work provides a potential chemical framework for nucleic acid probe design that could be explored in other molecular diagnostic systems.

title: Strategies for Preparing Migration‐Resistant Macromolecular Antioxidants
content:
A well‐defined “3C principle” covering compatibility, cocrystallization, and crosslinking was proposed for constructing macromolecular antioxidants with superior stability, which were prepared through ring‐opening metathesis polymerization or free radical‐type copolymerization.








ABSTRACT
Polymeric materials are susceptible to thermo‐oxidative degradation during melt processing and usage, which can be prevented using antioxidants. However, conventional small‐molecule antioxidants, such as phenolic antioxidants, are prone to migration, which compromises their long‐term effectiveness. To address this, for crystalline/semicrystalline polymers, we propose a systematic design strategy for macromolecular antioxidants based on the “3C principle” (Compatibility, cocrystallization, and crosslinking) to construct novel stabilizers with enhanced antioxidant performance and migration resistance. For noncrystalline polymers, macromolecular antioxidants satisfying only two of these criteria can also provide good antioxidant performance. Based on these design principles, three different types of macromolecular antioxidants were developed with structures tailored to the characteristics of commodity plastics, including polyethylene, polymethyl methacrylate, and polystyrene. This work provides a new approach for enhancing the service stability of polymeric materials and offers a broad molecular design strategy for functionalized polymer materials.

title: Revealing the Atomic‐Scale Structure of the Copper–Sulfuric Acid Interface
content:
How do acids interact with metallic surfaces? Using a multidisciplinary approach of electrodeposition and 3D‐printing, a novel approach of micro‐corrosion cells enables cryogenic atom probe tomography at the liquid‐solid interface of dilute sulfuric acid in contact with copper at different time and thermal conditions. 








ABSTRACT
Corrosion originates from atomistic reactions occurring at dynamic solid–liquid interfaces; however, direct experimental observation of these reactions has remained elusive due to the inability to preserve transient interfacial states during characterization. To refine corrosion models, advanced techniques capable of analyzing corrosion interfaces at the atomic scale are essential. Recent advancements in cryogenic‐atom probe tomography (cryo‐APT) enabled 3D nanoscale analysis of frozen liquid‐metal interfaces. However, challenges remain in sample preparation for cryo‐APT on metals undergoing corrosion. This study introduces a microcorrosion cell fabricated using localized electrodeposition in liquid (LEL), enabling atomic‐scale capture of liquid–metal reactions by integrating picoliter‐scale electrolytes encapsulated within sealed metallic microvessels, subsequently analyzed using cryo‐APT. This approach enables 3D, nanoscale mapping of corrosion reactions with simultaneous spatial, chemical, and temporal resolution. As a model system, copper exposed to aerated dilute sulphuric acid reveals temperature‐ and time‐dependent interfacial evolution, including nanoscale clustering of copper–sulphate species, enhanced ion pairing at elevated temperature, and the emergence of transient carbon‐based interfacial complexes inaccessible to conventional characterization methods. Beyond copper corrosion, the presented microcorrosion cell architecture establishes a strategy for interrogating confined electrochemical and degradation processes across a wide range of material–liquid systems, using a combination of microfabrication and cryo‐APT.

title: Phase Engineering of MoS2 for High‐Performance Anion Exchange Membrane Water and Glucose Electrolyzer
content:
A well‐engineered Fe, P‐MoS2 hybrid nanostructure was prepared via a hydrothermal process, demonstrating excellent efficiency and durability as an electrocatalyst for multifunctional water‐electrolysis activities. 








ABSTRACT
Water electrolysis for green hydrogen production is hindered by the high energy consumption of the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Replacing OER with the glucose oxidation reaction (GOR) using a phase‐engineered MoS2‐based electrocatalyst offers a promising route to lower the overall cell voltage while simultaneously valorizing biomass. Herein, Fe and P co‐doping induces a 2H‐to‐1T phase transition in MoS2, generating abundant sulfur vacancies and metallic conductivity. At high glucose coverage, electron transfer shifts from Fe to Mo sites, enabling selective GOR over OER. The Fe, P‐MoS2 catalyst delivers ultralow overpotentials of 98 mV for HER and 260 mV for OER, along with a low operating voltage of 1.30 V (vs. RHE) for GOR at 10 mA cm−2. In a full anion‐exchange membrane glucose electrolyzer (AEMGE), the Fe, P‐MoS2||Fe, P‐MoS2 configuration achieves cell voltages of 1.74 and 2.00 V at 0.5 and 1.0 A cm−2, respectively, substantially lower than the corresponding water electrolyzer (2.16 and 2.56 V), with excellent stability over 50 h. DFT calculations reveal that Fe/P co‐doping synergistically enhances charge carrier mobility and optimizes adsorption energies for glucose activation and intermediate conversion. This work highlights efficient hydrogen production alongside biomass upgrading with reduced energy consumption.

title: Controllable Template Assisted In Situ Perovskite Growth for Display Application
content:
A template assisted in situ crystallization strategy employs a bifunctional diamine ligand as a molecular bridge to grow CsPbX3 (X ‐ Cl, Br, I) perovskites within porous PET membranes. The engineered interface eliminates interfacial air gaps, enabling uniform pore filling, enhanced emission, exceptional stability, and inkjet‐printed full‐color RGB pixel arrays for flexible display applications.








ABSTRACT
Metal halide perovskites are compelling emitters for next‐generation optoelectronics, yet their translation into flexible display architectures remains limited by interfacial optical losses, non‐radiative recombination, and poor operational durability. Here we report a one‐step, template‐assisted in situ crystallization strategy that integrates CsPbX3 (X = Cl, Br, I) directly within a porous polyethylene terephthalate (PET) membrane. A bifunctional diamine ligand molecularly bridges the perovskite and polymer, directing crystallization, promoting uniform pore filling and eliminating interfacial air gaps. This chemically defined interface suppresses non‐radiative losses, increases light outcoupling from ∼13% to 36%, and yields a film‐state photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of 62%. The resulting perovskite‐integrated porous PET membrane retains ∼82% of its initial photoluminescence after 150 days under ambient conditions and exhibits a projected T50 of ∼10 000 h, establishing benchmark stability among in situ synthesized perovskite/polymer display‐class systems. It further preserves >90% emission under repeated bending and enables inkjet‐printed full‐color RGB pixel arrays with 70% NTSC gamut. Using a highly porous PET membrane (0.5 µm pore diameter), a luminance of 1050 nits are achieved, confirming that brightness scales with pore density and is substrate limited. These results establish active encapsulation as a practical route to stable, efficient and mechanically compliant perovskite display platforms.

title:
Competing Effects Modulate
the Rate of Poly(A) RNA
Deadenylation in a Biomolecular Condensate
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The unique solvent milieu found in biomolecular condensates can control cellular enzymatic reactions and shift reaction kinetics by modulating reactant concentrations, structural dynamics, and enzyme activities. Here, we explore the interplay of multiple regulatory factors within a condensate to control poly(A) RNA deadenylation, the first and rate-limiting step in mRNA turnover. The deadenylase CNOT7, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT deadenylation complex, localizes to protein- and RNA-rich granules and shows increased degradation activity in vitro in condensates formed by the C-terminal low-complexity disordered region of CAPRIN1, a component of many ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules. We use a combination of enzymatic assays, kinetic modeling, microscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations to deconvolute and define the components that underlie this enhancement. We found that enzyme and RNA are concentrated in condensates relative to buffer, which increases CNOT7 activity, while the equilibrium between CNOT7’s active and inactive states remains unchanged. The concentration-dependent increase in enzymatic rates is counterbalanced by a decrease in the enzyme’s catalytic efficiency, likely due to slower diffusion of CNOT7 and RNA within the condensates, which lessens the probability of enzyme–substrate complex formation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal CNOT7-CAPRIN1 interactions that rely on conserved CAPRIN1 sequence features, hinting at an evolutionarily conserved role for CAPRIN1 condensation. With this quantitative kinetic analysis, we describe the multifaceted mechanism behind regulation of CNOT7 deadenylation by a condensate environment.</jats:p>

Journal of
the American
Chemical Society

title:
Coexisting Liquid-,
Glassy-, and Crystal-like
Phonons in a Crystalline Solid
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As main states of matter, crystal, glass, and liquid manifest themselves in distinct transverse collective atomic vibrations. In contrast to crystals where transverse phonons are well-defined throughout Brillouin zones, glasses and liquids process such motions in long and/or short wavelength limits, respectively. Considerable efforts have been made to experimentally probe transverse phonon behavior in these highly anharmonic and disordered materials in pursuit of a universal framework for thermal transport. In this work, inelastic neutron scattering on AgCrSe2 single crystals reveals liquid-, glassy-, and crystal-like phonon features along different crystallographic directions. In particular, the liquid-like behavior is attributed to the significant softening and scattering arising from the nesting effect and dynamical atomic disorder while the glassy-like behavior is due to the selective disorder effect. Our findings challenge conventional boundaries between states of matter at the level of atomic dynamics and establish a materials platform for unifying the thermal transport theories across different states.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
Water-Cluster-Expanded
Interpenetrated Covalent Organic
Frameworks Create High-Affinity Coordination Microenvironments for
Efficient Strontium Capture
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The efficient capture of radioactive strontium (Sr2+) from nuclear-contaminated water is of critical importance for environmental safety and public health protection. Three-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (3D COFs) with multi-interpenetrated architectures offer the potential for multidentate synergistic coordination toward target Sr2+. However, the confined internal environment arising from uncontrolled multi-interpenetration often restricts coordination freedom, while the concomitant reduction in pore size and obstruction of transport channels impose significant kinetic limitations on the adsorption process. Herein, we report a water-cluster-induced framework swelling strategy implemented in our synthesized 3D TB-COF adsorbent. This approach simultaneously establishes a multisource coordination environment that enhances both Sr2+ affinity and selectivity, and expands the pore channels to eliminate transport barriers, reduce mass-transfer resistance, and improve active-site accessibility. The water-expanded TB-COF adsorbent achieves a record-high maximum adsorption amount (qmax = 346.2 mg g–1) and excellent selectivity in simulated nuclear wastewater, alongside outstanding radiation tolerance. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the superior Sr2+ recognition originates from the water-cluster-modulated coordination space constructed by three adjacent networks. This work provides a general design strategy for developing advanced 3D interpenetrated COF adsorbents toward environmental remediation of nuclear contamination.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of
the American
Chemical Society

title:
Mechanically Tunable
Quantum Transport in Graphene
Nanoribbons with Antiaromatic Motifs
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nonbenzenoid graphene nanoribbons provide a versatile platform for tailoring electronic structures beyond conventional benzenoid π-conjugated systems, yet the impact of their topology on quantum transport remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate electrical conductance through suspended ladder phenylene nanoribbons containing antiaromatic four-membered rings using scanning tunneling microscope lifting spectroscopy. As the nanoribbon is progressively detached from the substrate, differential conductance measurements reveal successive charge-state transitions accompanied by alternating Kondo resonances, demonstrating the dynamic generation of localized spins in an intrinsically closed-shell nanoribbon. Density functional theory calculations show that the antiaromatic topology reduces the HOMO–LUMO gap and induces a pronounced length dependence of the occupied frontier orbitals, which shift progressively toward and eventually across the electrode Fermi level with increasing suspended length, driving successive charge-state transitions. The transport behavior is quantitatively described within a double-barrier tunneling framework incorporating charge quantization and many-body interactions. These results suggest an antiaromaticity-driven mechanism for charge-state evolution and propose antiaromaticity as a molecular design principle for controlling charge and spin states in nonbenzenoid carbon nanostructures.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of
the American
Chemical Society

title:
Geometry-Programmed
Connectivity Enables Predictive
Assembly of Diamond-Family Colloidal Crystals
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The predictive assembly of open colloidal crystals requires encoding specific connectivity rules into building blocks that are otherwise isotropic and lack inherent directionality. Here we introduce a geometry-programmed connectivity strategy in which spatial confinement, rather than surface patterning or lattice templating, programs not only particle coordination but also the accessible bonding arrangement that governs network connectivity. We implement this concept using tetrahedral DNA origami frameworks that confine DNA-functionalized spherical particles and restrict their accessible bonding pathways to four tetrahedrally arranged patches, thereby converting isotropic colloids into effective tetravalent building blocks with geometrically prescribed connectivity. A geometric hard-contact model translates these confinement-defined connectivity rules and the linker-defined interaction range into coordination regimes and lattice symmetry, yielding a predictive phase diagram. Guided by this model, we experimentally realize diamond-family colloidal crystals featuring the coexistence of cubic diamond and double diamond phases, as well as zinc blende and double zinc blende phases. Photonic band-structure calculations predict that the experimentally realized cubic diamond and zinc blende topologies can support complete PBGs in the deep-ultraviolet regime. We thus establish a predictive form of colloidal topological engineering, in which confinement geometry programs local connectivity and selects emergent crystal topology.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
A Predictive Betaine
Organocatalyst Platform for Asymmetric
1,3-Dipolar Cycloadditions Enabled by Interaction-Aware Modeling
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Predicting enantioselectivity in asymmetric (organo)catalysis remains a longstanding challenge, particularly in systems where stereocontrol is governed by weak, highly flexible, and substrate-dependent noncovalent interactions. In such regimes, simplified transition-state-based DFT analysis can become unreliable due to the presence of multiple low-energy conformations, competing binding modes, and alternative reaction pathways. We introduce a previously unexplored chiral imidazolium/aryloxide betaine organocatalyst platform for asymmetric 1,3-dipolar cycloadditions of CH-acidic imines with maleimides that operates with exceptional efficiency, reaching turnover numbers of up to 3000 while maintaining high enantiocontrol. To overcome the limitations of transition-state-guided catalyst optimization and enable predictive control beyond the limits of mechanistic intuition, we combined combinatorial catalyst-substrate screening with descriptor-based statistical modeling. Analysis of the resulting data set reveals that no single catalyst is universally optimal across substrate space; instead, enantioselectivity is governed by a catalyst-substrate matching effect. The resulting models identify the molecular features associated with selectivity and enable prospective prediction of enantioselectivity for previously unseen catalysts and a structurally distinct substrate class. These findings establish highly productive metal-free azomethine ylide cycloadditions and demonstrate how interaction-aware data-driven models can provide predictive control in complex asymmetric catalytic systems.</jats:p>

Journal of
the American
Chemical Society

title:
Orbital
Discreteness Modulates Electron-Counting Adsorption
Trends in Atomically Dispersed Catalysts
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Understanding adsorption at atomically dispersed catalytic sites remains a central challenge, as conventional d-band theory fails to describe emerging molecular-like electronic structures in single-atom systems. Here, we identify a unified electronic framework that bridges metallic single-atom alloys and nitrogen-coordinated graphene single-atom catalysts (transition-metal atoms coordinated by four nitrogen atoms in graphene, TM-N4-Gr), connecting band-like and ligand-field-dominated regimes through a common orbital-filling picture. Systematic density functional theory calculations for C, N, and O adsorption show that adsorption-energy minima in both platforms exhibit a common ten-electron-like counting trend across transition-metal dopants. This behavior originates from molecular-orbital-like filling of dopant-adsorbate hybrid states, linking electron-counting behavior in metallic and coordination-stabilized single-atom environments. Crucially, orbital discreteness is identified as an important factor regulating how this electron-counting trend manifests. In TM-N4-Gr systems, localized d states promote more distinct bonding and antibonding states, leading to enhanced sensitivity to electron filling beyond the optimal electron count, whereas metallic hosts induce electronic delocalization that smooths this response. These results establish a unified orbital-filling framework in which adsorption is governed by the interplay between electron counting and orbital discreteness, providing a general physical basis for atomically dispersed catalysis.</jats:p>

Journal of
the American
Chemical Society

title:
A Bioinspired
Gold–Chalcogen Bonding Synergistic
Catalysis Platform: Switchable Activation and Dynamic Functional Group
Sampling
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Enzymes achieve exceptional catalytic efficiency by leveraging proximity effects and cooperative interactions, inspiring the design of artificial catalysis systems. However, mimicking this concept has been constrained by rigid activation modes and limited functional group interactions. Inspired by chalcogen-bonding metalloenzymes, we report the design and application of a synergistic gold–chalcogen bonding catalysis platform featuring switchable activation centers and dynamic functional group sampling. This platform employs a rationally designed bifunctional gold–chalcogen bonding catalyst, in which the activation center switches between chalcogen and gold sites, while the complementary moiety provides proximity effect. Chalcogen bonding enables dynamic functional group sampling that allows the catalyst to orthogonally interact with various functional groups, including similar ones such as alkenes and alkynes, thereby triggering unique reactivity. Proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that this platform enables the direct synthesis of sterically hindered ethers via alcohol addition to multisubstituted alkenes, including fully substituted variants. Moreover, this strategy extends to new polymerization reactions of tryptamine and alkyne derivatives via a cyclization pathway. Control experiments confirm that none of these transformations proceed under gold or chalcogen bonding catalysis alone, underscoring the unique and synergistic nature of this platform. Given its high activity and broad potential, the concept of chalcogen-bonding metal synergistic catalysis is expected to find broad applications in developing diverse reactions.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of
the American
Chemical Society

title:
Charge-to-Mass Ratio
Regulation of Solvated Li+ Clusters for Ultrafast-Charging
Lithium Battery Electrolytes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Extreme fast charging of high-energy lithium batteries is limited by coupled Li+ transport, interfacial desolvation, and electrode degradation. Here, we introduce q/Mcluster as a composition-derived prescreening descriptor, where q is the assigned charge number of the Li-centered carrier (+1 here) and Mcluster is the abundance-weighted composition mass of the cationic clusters in the four most populated solvent-separated ion-pair (SSIP) configurations. A higher q/Mcluster identifies a lower average cluster composition mass and prioritizes electrolyte candidates for transport and electrochemical testing. Guided by this descriptor, we develop a methyl acetate/fluoroethylene carbonate (MA/FEC) electrolyte that favors MA-rich solvated Li+ clusters with lower composition mass and dynamic ligand exchange, while FEC supports interphase stabilization. Simulations and experiments show weaker Li+–solvent association, a lower calculated cluster ligand-removal energy, and faster Li+ diffusion in the optimized formulation. It enables stable operation for 1000 cycles at 15C and 500 cycles in a 1 Ah pouch cell under 3C charging. Composition and cross-family controls support complementary roles for MA-regulated solvation and FEC-derived interphase stabilization, while revealing limits to a single-parameter ranking. Thus, q/Mcluster helps prioritize formulations for independent transport, interfacial, and electrochemical validation.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of
the American
Chemical Society

title:
Interfacial
Fueling with Physical Autocatalysis Programs
Transient Crystallization and Nonconventional Fluorescence
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chemically fueled self-assembly generates transient structures, but coupling spatially controlled product formation to phase evolution remains challenging, particularly for crystallization. Here we introduce a two-phase interfacial fueling strategy in which a hydrophobic anhydride fuel forms an oil phase and reacts with an aqueous precursor to generate amphiphiles locally at the oil–water interface. In the micelle-forming regime, the resulting assemblies enhance interfacial fuel transport and promote further amphiphile formation, establishing physical positive feedback. Coupling this process to ester hydrolysis enables transient micellar assembly. Decreasing product solubility redirects the same fueling network toward transient crystallization. In this regime, poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) shifts the apparent crystallization boundary and regulates crystal growth and aggregation, with nuclear magnetic resonance titration and molecular simulations supporting polymer–amphiphile association. An alternative anionic polymer partially reproduces aggregation suppression, indicating that this behavior is not exclusive to a single polymer. Counterion-dependent fluorescence provides a label-free optical readout of transient crystallization. Across the tested anhydride–ester systems, these results establish a design framework linking fuel partitioning, product solubility, and intermolecular association to transient structural and optical responses. Extension to other chemical systems requires compatible phase behavior and a suitable balance between product-generation and deactivation kinetics.</jats:p>

Journal of
the American
Chemical Society

title:
Programmable Directional
Assembly of Hydrogen-Bonded
Lead Organic Chalcogenolates
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Controlling the directional assembly of metal organic chalcogenolates (MOCs) with atomic precision remains a synthetic challenge yet represents a critical step toward advancing their programmable syntheses and property investigations. Herein, we present a “hydrogen-bond-directed assembly” strategy to drive the formation of single-crystalline, hydrogen-bonded lead organic chalcogenolates (H-LOCs), offering an ideal platform for elucidating their structure–property relationships. By strategically functionalizing thiophenol with regiochemically or electronically distinct substituents, we achieved precise control at the ligand–ligand interface, yielding six distinct H-LOC architectures mediated by interlayer, intralayer, or cooperative hybrid hydrogen-bonding interactions. These programmed hydrogen-bonding interactions play an essential role in crystal growth, enabling the formation of large single crystals of two-dimensional (2D) LOCs. Combined structural and optical characterizations reveal a linear correlation between the ligand electronic effects and optical bandgaps of the materials, culminating in a narrow bandgap of 1.55 eV for the most electron-donating substituent. Most importantly, the reversible nature of these interfacial hydrogen bonds endows the H-LOCs with excellent solution-processability, allowing them to be fabricated into highly stable films with ambient durability exceeding two months─thereby unlocking their potential for optoelectronic devices.</jats:p>

title:
Glycosaminoglycans
Promote Amyloid-β
Aggregation via Multivalent, pH-Dependent Interactions
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are polyanionic polysaccharides that colocalize with amyloid deposits in Alzheimer’s disease, yet their mechanistic contribution to aggregation remains unclear. Here, we show that GAGs function as pH-responsive electrostatic scaffolds that selectively accelerate Aβ(1–42) aggregation under mildly acidic, early endosomal-like conditions but not at neutral pH. Combining experimental and computational approaches, we identify protonated N-terminal histidines as key determinants of GAG binding. Weak interactions between GAGs and the charged N-terminal region of Aβ promote conformational rearrangements that bring peptides into proximity and expose adjacent hydrophobic aggregation-prone segments, thereby facilitating peptide clustering. Kinetic analyses reveal that aggregation is enhanced in a way consistent with an apparent increase in effective peptide concentration, accelerating nucleation without altering the dominant aggregation pathway. Systematic variation of GAG chain length and sulfation level further demonstrates that aggregation enhancement requires a threshold degree of multivalency, consistent with a clustering-driven mechanism. Together, these findings establish a framework in which pH-dependent polyelectrolyte interactions act as molecular triggers of amyloid nucleation and define the physicochemical parameters that govern when GAGs transition from passive interaction partners to active promoters of Aβ aggregation, providing insight into how cellular microenvironments may regulate the earliest stages of Alzheimer’s disease pathology.</jats:p>

title:
A Cationic Ruthenium
Olefin Metathesis Catalyst Supported
on Weakly Coordinating Silica
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Silica functionalized with Lewis acidic silylium aluminate ion-pairs ([iPr3Si][(RFO)3Al–OSi≡] (RF = C(CF3)3)) abstract chloride from the second-generation Grubbs-Hoveyda catalyst (SIMes)Cl2Ru=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4) (GH-II) to form supported [(SIMes)ClRu=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4)][(RFO)3Al–OSi≡] (1) and iPr3SiCl. Solid-state NMR measurements at 100 K, desorption of Ru from the support, and X-ray adsorption spectroscopy (XAS) are consistent with formation of a monomeric Ru-benzylidene cation that is electrostatically immobilized on the modified silica surface. 1 is active and selective in ring closing metathesis (RCM), self-metathesis, ring opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP), acyclic diene metathesis (ADMET), cross metathesis, and ethenolysis reactions. 1 is generally more active than cationic [(SIMes)ClRu=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4)]2[BArF4]2 (GH-II+; BArF4 = tetrakis(3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)borate) in these reactions and gives higher yields with higher selectivity than neutral GH-II under equivalent conditions. DFT calculations comparing models of GH-II+ and 1 suggest that cationic Ru=CH2+ is stabilized by interactions with the anion and accounts for the increase in reaction rates observed using 1 compared to GH-II+.</jats:p>

title:
Physicochemical Reaction
Control Enables Molar-Mass-Selective
Macromolecular Electrolysis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tailoring molar-mass distributions postsynthetically remains a long-standing challenge in polymer chemistry that conventionally requires the synthesis of dedicated polymer libraries. Here, we show that heterogeneous macromolecular electrolysis can edit polymer-molar-mass distributions on demand from a single prepolymer sample, tuning number-average molar mass (Mn) from 60 to 902 kg mol–1 and dispersity (Đ) from 1.3 to 7. This capability arises from a previously unrecognized mode of selectivity where heterogeneous electroreduction mediates polymer substrate reactivity through physicochemical reaction control. In this electrolytic transformation, molar-mass-dependent transport physically affects the rate of redox activation with an approximately linear dependence on the diffusion coefficient of these macromolecules. This leads to preferential activation of lower-molar-mass polymers, which is a consequence of more rapidly diffusing species having preferential access to the electrode interface. Moreover, we show that during this macromolecular electrolysis, every redox-active unit on a single polymer chain is activated prior to polymer desorption from the working electrode, which is a distinct manifestation of physicochemical control. This stands in contrast to conventional postpolymerization transformations that are inherently stochastic in nature, where target units on individual polymer chains statistically react and reactions on large polymers are more likely to occur. Electrode identity controls polymer–electrode interactions. Strong radical adsorption to graphite drives complete activation of individual chains before desorption. On reticulated vitreous carbon, adsorption is weaker and reactivity reverts to stochastic activation, which causes the molar-mass distribution to shift gradually over the course of electrolysis. We leveraged these differences to arbitrarily tune molar-mass distributions postsynthetically by selectively deconstructing prototypical N-(methacryloxy)phthalimide methacrylate copolymers. These findings establish interfacial electrochemical environments as a platform for molar-mass-selective macromolecular transformations and introduce a new axis of selectivity in synthetic polymer chemistry.</jats:p>

title: Light-Driven Hydrogenation–Dehydrogenation of Toluene–Methylcyclohexane by Plasmonic Photocatalysis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The development of an efficient and reversible hydrogen storage and transport system is crucial for a sustainable hydrogen economy. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHCs) offer a potential solution due to their high hydrogen storage density and ease of transport, but conventional thermal approaches for the hydrogenation and dehydrogenation of LOHCs remain heavily reliant on harsh operating conditions. Here, we demonstrate a plasmonic photocatalysis approach for toluene hydrogenation to methylcyclohexane and methylcyclohexane dehydrogenation to toluene under substantially milder conditions. We observe changes in reaction orders and substantial reductions in activation barriers by 0.34 and 1.11 eV for toluene hydrogenation and methylcyclohexane dehydrogenation, respectively, as compared to thermocatalysis due to the role of hot carriers. Both reactions exhibit high activity, stability (&gt;70 h), and excellent selectivity (&gt;95%), offering a sustainable pathway for on-demand hydrogen storage and release.</jats:p>
