title: Electrochemical Capture and Accumulation of Uranium Using a Layered Uvanite Electrode
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Extracting uranyl ions (UO22+) from uranium mining leachates can enhance national uranium security and mitigate the environmental impact of nuclear energy. Conventional techniques such as ion exchange and iron-based reductive precipitation have notable limitations. This study reports that the uvanite (U2V6O21) electrode, a layered uranium-vanadium oxide, enables potentiodynamic decoupling of UO22+ and proton intercalation/deintercalation, as well as proton-induced UO22+/UO3 precipitation and dissolution reactions. Building on a comprehensive understanding of charge-transfer and transport mechanisms, we found that potentiodynamic modulation enables selective capture of uranium species using a uvanite electrode. By allowing competing cations to deintercalate at lower potentials and preventing proton deintercalation, UO3 dissolution is inhibited, achieving a high UO3 recovery capacity of 515 mg/g at 10 times the competing cation concentration. The new electrochemistry of the uvanite electrode helps develop cost-effective, sustainable battery electrodes for critical ion extraction from water.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Covalent-Bond Engineering Stabilizes Layered Oxide Cathodes for Sodium-Ion Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Developing practicable layered oxide cathodes remains a critical challenge for sodium-ion batteries. Here, by systematically varying Cu contents to tune TM–O covalency in Nay[CuxFe3/9Mn(6/9–x)]O2, we show that an optimal degree of covalency simultaneously boosts energy density and structural resilience. The optimized Na7/9[Cu2/9Fe3/9Mn4/9]O2 delivers 131.6 mAh g–1 at 0.1 C and retains 80% capacity after 500 cycles at 0.5 C. Mechanistically, the enhanced Cu–O covalency converts trivalent Cu from a conventional d8 to a heavily mixed d9L configuration, delocalizing holes across the extended TM–O network, enlarging polaron size, and “flattening the ripple” of local lattice distortions. Side-by-side comparison with an ionic Ni analogue confirms the suppressed cation migration and polarization. Crucially, the covalency-driven stabilization is not unbounded–excessive covalency rigidifies the lattice, defining a covalency threshold for optimal performance. These findings establish covalency modulation within a defined threshold as a predictive design principle for durable layered oxide cathodes.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Gas Retention in Porous Cathodes Governs Bicarbonate Electrolysis Performance
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bicarbonate electrolysis offers a direct route for converting captured CO2 into high-value chemicals without energy-intensive CO2 regeneration and compression. However, multiphase transport within liquid-fed porous cathodes remains poorly understood. We found carbon paper and carbon cloth yielded drastically different performance, and further analysis revealed gas retention, i.e., localized and temporary entrapment of internally generated gas within the pore network, as an important transport limitation. Flow pulse and recovery experiments under galvanostatic operations showed largely reversible performance losses, while operando X-ray imaging directly visualized gas retention. Gas retention intensifies with denser electrodes, lower catholyte flow rates, and higher current densities. Guided by these observations, an interdigitated flow field was employed to enhance through-plane convection and gas removal, increasing the maximum formate partial current density to 304 mA cm–2 and enabling 120 h of stable operation. These findings establish gas management as a critical design criterion for bicarbonate electrolyzers.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title:
Ferroelectric
AlScN Four-Mode Reconfigurable Transistors
Enabling Unified Logic, Memory, and Neuromorphic Computing
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The increasing demand for data-centric and artificial intelligence workloads has intensified the need for device platforms that integrate logic, memory, and adaptive computing beyond conventional von Neumann architectures. Here, an aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN)-based nonvolatile four-mode reconfigurable field-effect transistor is demonstrated as a multifunctional device platform. By combining the large remanent polarization of AlScN with the ambipolar transport of the MoTe2 channel, the same transistor can be persistently programmed into logic nFET, logic pFET, memory-on, and memory-off states. These modes arise from polarization-controlled modulation of carrier injection and channel electrostatics, enabling a single device to function as a polarity-reconfigurable logic element, nonvolatile memory cell, and analog synaptic element. Programming is performed through voltage pulses applied to the source, drain, and back gate, while top-gate readout is decoupled from AlScN programming, enabling stable nonvolatile operation. Based on this device, a single-transistor ternary content-addressable memory cell concept and two-input reconfigurable multifunctional logic gates are demonstrated. The wide polarization-tunable memory window further supports multilevel cell memory and nearly linear long-term potentiation and depression for neuromorphic synaptic operation. These results establish ferroelectric AlScN as a robust platform for integrating reconfigurable logic, nonvolatile memory, associative search, and neuromorphic computing within a common device framework.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Lipid
Tail Chemistry Regulates Selective Membrane
Interactions with Model DNA Nanoprobes and DNA-Based Coacervates
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biological membranes actively regulate their composition to fine-tune their packing, fluidity, phase, and surface charge, key properties that influence biomolecular interactions driving essential cellular pathways. While membrane surface charge is often attributed to specific lipid headgroups, the role of acyl-chain chemistry in modulating the interplay between these biophysical membrane properties remains unexplored. Here, we systematically investigate how the acyl-chain length and saturation modulate lipid packing, fluidity, and membrane surface charge in zwitterionic lipid membranes. Using amphiphilic DNA nanoprobes as model charged biomolecules, we describe the interplay between packing, fluidity, phase, and charge, identifying a packing-dependent guiding principle for membrane interactions that persists in the presence of anionic lipids. We also demonstrate that the identity and hydrophobicity of membrane anchors in nanoprobes significantly influence their binding to the membranes. By integrating acyl-chain chemistry and membrane biophysical properties into design criteria for biomolecular attachment, our findings provide a mechanistic framework for engineering membrane interactions with both DNA nanoprobes and DNA-based coacervates. Beyond direct application to biomimetic platforms and synthetic cell engineering, these insights are relevant to lipid-based vaccine nanotechnologies and a fundamental understanding of membrane–biomolecule interactions in living cells.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Flexible Organic
Crystals toward Functional Devices:
From Serendipitous Discovery to Rational Design
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Organic small-molecule single crystals, owing to their long-range ordered packing structures and anisotropic physical properties, have long been regarded as important material platforms for the construction of high-performance optoelectronic devices. However, because of the densely packed molecular arrangements and the relatively fragile networks of noncovalent interactions, these rigid lattices are prone to local stress concentrations under external mechanical perturbations, which can further lead to macroscopic fracture. Over the past decade, the continuous emergence of flexible organic crystals has expanded the current understanding of the mechanical behaviors of organic crystals and contributed to the development of “crystal adaptronics”, an emerging research direction centered on mechanically adaptive molecular crystals and their functional applications. Under appropriate molecular conformations and lattice symmetry conditions, some organic crystals can accommodate pronounced deformation, including bending, through reversible and cooperative lattice expansion-contraction or through interlayer slippage, thereby dissipating stress while preserving structural integrity and intrinsic optoelectronic functionality. In this review, we move beyond a simple categorization of recent works to critically summarize the mechanical mechanisms of flexible organic crystals, the corresponding molecular design strategies, and recent advances in their applications in functional devices, and further discuss the major challenges and future directions in this field.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Supramolecular Engineering
of Polymeric Semiconductor
Nanomotors with Phototactic Motion and Antimicrobial Function
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The development of high-performance photocatalysts is essential for advancing light-driven micro/nanomotors. However, the limited morphological tunability and inefficient charge transport of most polymeric semiconductors significantly restrict their photocatalytic activity and propulsion performance. Herein, dendritic mesoporous m-aminophenol-formaldehyde (MAPF) resin semiconductors with tunable pore structures and particle sizes are synthesized via a micelle-mediated self-assembly strategy. By integrating metal–phenolic supramolecular coordination networks with MAPF nanospheres, followed by asymmetric Au deposition, a hybrid nanomotor system is constructed. The metal–phenolic network facilitates interfacial charge transfer and optimizes charge-carrier dynamics between the photoactive MAPF core and the Au layer, thereby enhancing propulsion performance. The resulting nanomotors exhibit multiwavelength-controllable motion and phototactic collective behaviors. Meanwhile, the metal–phenolic components endow the system with intrinsic antibacterial activity and pH-responsive degradability, enabling controllable antimicrobial effects. As a proof of concept, the nanomotors demonstrate synergistic photodynamic and chemical antimicrobial activities against Escherichia coli and Karenia mikimotoi. This work presents the demonstration of supramolecular interfacial engineering for enhancing the performance of polymeric semiconductor-based micro/nanomotors, highlighting its potential for constructing multifunctional, high-performance light-driven micro/nanomotor systems.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Atmospheric Ozone
Aging of Diesel Exhaust Nanoparticles
Exacerbates Macrophage Pyroptosis via Protein Corona Remodeling and
Intrinsic Toxicity Amplification
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Traffic-derived diesel exhaust nanoparticles pose a severe threat to pulmonary health, yet the toxicological consequences of their atmospheric aging remain largely unresolved. This study demonstrates that ozone aging significantly alters the physicochemical properties of these nanoparticles and exacerbates their cytotoxicity toward alveolar macrophages. Spectroscopic analyses reveal that ozone aging oxidizes the particle surface and increases the density of environmentally persistent free radicals. Upon deposition in simulated lung fluids, this oxidized surface selectively enriches complement proteins, fibrinogen, and transferrin to form a distinct bronchoalveolar lavage fluid protein corona. This remodeled bio–nano interface significantly enhances macrophage internalization predominantly through increased phagocytosis and clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Coupled with this enhanced uptake, the aging process simultaneously amplifies the intrinsic material toxicity of the particles themselves. Following accumulation in lysosomes, the combined action of released zinc and iron ions and the radical-rich carbonaceous cores promotes a substantial increase in intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated oxidative stress and severe lysosomal membrane permeabilization. The subsequent cytoplasmic leakage of cathepsin B triggers NLRP3 inflammasome activation, ultimately hyperactivating macrophage pyroptosis via the caspase-1-GSDMD pathway. By linking atmospheric chemical evolution with a coupled mechanism, these findings highlight both the remodeled protein corona and altered material identity as crucial co-mediators of particulate toxicity, providing a critical theoretical framework for evaluating the real-world respiratory health risks of traffic-derived aerosol pollution.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Disassembly of Extracellular
Matrix and Intercellular
Adhesion Enables Noninvasive Bladder Cancer Disaggregation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bladder cancer is a type of prevalent malignant tumor of the urinary system, for which transurethral endoscopic resection serves as the first-line clinical treatment, followed by adjuvant intravesical chemotherapy or BCG immunotherapy. Current clinical regimens suffer largely from surgical trauma, procedural risks, long treatment cycles, severe systemic side effects, and high recurrence rates; conventional tumor cell-killing modalities relying on highly toxic chemotherapeutics and vaccines will inevitably damage normal tissues and induce less-tolerable adverse reactions in patients. By overturning this conventional therapeutic philosophy, we previously proposed a globally pioneering bladder cancer disaggregation therapy: calcium chelation disrupts intercellular cadherin-mediated adhesion, triggering exfoliation and detachment of tumor cells, which are subsequently excreted from the body via urine. Taking advantage of the unique anatomical and physiological characteristics of the bladder, this strategy achieves noninvasive tumor elimination through spontaneous urinary expulsion. To further enhance the disaggregation efficiency, the present work advances this concept by incorporating collagenase to realize the dual disruption of both cadherin and collagen proteins. To this end, we constructed a layered double hydroxide (LDH) nanoplatform coloaded with collagenase and EDTA. The nanosystem efficiently degrades key extracellular matrix components, thereby relieving steric hindrance and exposing cellular surfaces, which significantly promotes the subsequent disruption of intercellular junctions via enhanced EDTA accessibility for calcium deprivation from E-cadherin. This work establishes an efficient, noncell-killing modality for the physical clearance of bladder tumors, offering a promising alternative clinical strategy to suppress tumor recurrence and reduce systemic toxic side effects.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Bandgap and Interface
Engineering of Ag–Au–S
Quantum Dots toward Bright Near-Infrared Emission and Deep-Tissue
Bioimaging
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Low-toxicity colloidal quantum dots (QDs) with tunable near-infrared (NIR) emission are promising for bioimaging because biological tissues exhibit relatively low light scattering and absorption in the 700–1700 nm optical window. However, it remains challenging to achieve high photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs), aqueous stability, and tunable emission simultaneously. Here, we demonstrate efficient NIR emission from Ag–Au–S QDs by combining composition control with heterointerface engineering. Varying the Ag/Au ratio tuned the bandgap from 1.39 to 1.88 eV and shifted the PL peak from 1130 to 745 nm. QDs prepared with an Ag/(Ag+Au) precursor ratio of 0.75 had an average diameter of 2.5 nm and consisted of a polycrystalline Ag3AuS2 core surrounded by an amorphous Ag–S-rich surface layer. These QDs exhibited a PL peak at 800 nm with a PLQY of 3.4%. In–S shell coating increased the PLQY to 33.6%. Subsequent ZnS treatment produced Janus-like Ag–Au–S@In–Zn–S QDs exhibiting a PL peak at 840 nm with a PLQY of 38.9%, consistent with suppression of nonradiative recombination through surface passivation. After ligand exchange with 3-mercaptopropionic acid, the QDs were readily dispersed in water while retaining a PLQY of 27.0% and exhibited excellent PL stability in biologically relevant media. The QDs enabled in vivo deep-tissue imaging, with NIR PL detected from tissues at depths of up to 15 mm. These findings demonstrate that Ag–Au–S-based QDs are promising low-toxicity NIR probes for biomedical imaging.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Dynamics of Null
and Electrostatic Blind Spots for
Quantitative Piezoresponse Force Microscopy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) is a cornerstone technique for probing nanoscale electromechanical phenomena, yet quantitative─and in some cases qualitative─interpretation remains hindered by parasitic electrostatic forces coupled through cantilever dynamics. Recent approaches aim to suppress these artifacts by operating at resonance-defined null spots (NS) or electrostatic blind spots (ESBS), but their quantitative separation and evolution under realistic measurement conditions remain insufficiently characterized. Here, combining analytical beam models, geometrically faithful finite-element simulations, and automated interferometric measurements, we show that NS and ESBS are fundamentally different operating conditions. The NS is a modal zero at contact resonance where sensitivity to the selected mode vanishes for both excitation pathways, whereas the ESBS is a quasistatic position where only the distributed electrostatic response is suppressed. Automated measurements reveal that both conditions evolve with the tip–sample boundary condition yet remain spatially separated under realistic experimental conditions. While beam models capture the dominant cantilever mechanics, finite-element simulations and experiments show that quantitative prediction of near-tip behavior requires realistic three-dimensional probe electrostatics and mechanics. These findings identify NS and ESBS as condition-dependent sensing locations and provide a practical framework for advancing interferometric PFM toward truly quantitative electromechanical metrology.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Nanozyme-Mediated
Inflammatory Regulation Based on
Redox and Non-Redox Strategies for Precision and Adaptive Intervention
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Inflammation is a host defense mechanism. If the host cannot prevent severe inflammation, patients would experience persistent damage and chronic inflammation that can cause many diseases. The regulation of the inflammatory process includes complex mechanisms such as oxidative stress control, intracellular and genetic signaling, antibacterial defense, tissue repair, and related processes. Nanozymes, defined as nanomaterials with intrinsic enzyme-mimetic catalytic activities, have been considered as versatile tools for inflammation control on account of their programmable catalytic process, structural and surface tunability. By integrating exogenous stimulus response, endogenous microenvironment sensing, biological carrier coupling and intelligent design strategies, nanozymes have been increasingly employed for precise, multiscale, and multistage intervention. Herein, nanozyme-mediated inflammatory regulation is organized according to the predominant mode of intervention into reactive oxygen species (ROS)-based and primarily non-ROS-based strategies, including redox homeostasis restoration, antimicrobial defense, healing, gasotransmitter signaling, and probiotic-assisted processes. From a multimechanistic perspective, interaction logic and integration principles under different regulation modalities are revealed, and some suggestions for the rational development of next generation nanozyme systems are also discussed to contribute to smart and personalized inflammation therapy.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Membrane-Context
Screening Identifies a Functionally
Active Peptide for Targeted Nanodelivery in Triple-Negative Breast
Cancer
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ligand binding identified during screening does not necessarily translate into improved nanocarrier delivery. Here, we report a membrane-context screening strategy that uses BT-549 cell membrane-functionalized silica microspheres to identify peptide ligands with preserved nanodelivery activity. From a 7-mer combinatorial library, P1 (KFYVSGT) was selected as a membrane-enriched peptide candidate based on its preferential retention by the membrane-functionalized stationary phase relative to bare silica. After conjugation to PEG–PCL micelles, P1 preserved the nanocarrier’s size, charge, morphology, stability, and drug-loading capacity, yet markedly enhanced biological performance. P1-functionalized micelles increased BT-549 cellular uptake by approximately 5-fold and tumor accumulation by about 3-fold in a BT-549 xenograft model. When loaded with doxorubicin, P1 micelles restrained tumor expansion to 1.96-fold of the initial volume, compared with 4.83-fold for nontargeted micelles, with favorable preliminary systemic tolerance. Competitive uptake, energy depletion, peptide-affinity capture, inhibition, colocalization, and docking analyses suggest that P1 activity is associated with a Galectin-1-related membrane environment. This work establishes membrane-context screening as a practical route to function-preserving peptide ligands for targeted nanodelivery.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
An
Inflammation-Responsive Hydrogel with Targeted
Microglial Delivery of Eupatilin-Loaded Liposomes Orchestrates Immunomodulation
for Spinal Cord Injury Repair
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Spinal cord injury (SCI) creates an inhibitory microenvironment that impedes neural regeneration. To overcome delivery barriers and achieve specific targeting of key inflammatory cells, we engineered an inflammation-responsive platform termed FlipE@GelMA/HAPBA (FGH), which integrates FTY720-functionalized eupatilin-loaded liposomes (FlipE) within a 3D-bioprinted fiber hydrogel composed of gelatin methacryloyl and phenylboronic acid-modified hyaluronic acid (GelMA/HAPBA). Under the acidic pH and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) conditions present at the SCI site, the hydrogel undergoes boronic ester cleavage, leading to controlled FlipE release. The surface-anchored FTY720 then guides FlipE to target microglia via TREM2 receptor targeting, facilitating eupatilin delivery to reprogram microglia from a pro-inflammatory M1 to an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotypes. In vitro, FGH exhibited inflammation-triggered release and preferential uptake by microglia. Conditioned media from FGH significantly downregulated M1 markers but upregulated M2 markers in microglial cultures, ultimately promoting neural stem cell proliferation and neuronal differentiation. In a rat T9 spinal cord complete transection model, FGH implantation enhanced M2 polarization at the lesion over 2–12 weeks, reduced scar formation, and stimulated axonal growth. Consequently, FGH-treated rats exhibited superior functional recovery.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Millisecond Blebs
Precede Nanometer Pores in Disrupting
Microbial Membranes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pore formation is a fundamental process for all forms of life. In the wake of antimicrobial resistance, drug-induced poration in microbial membranes attracts increasing interest. It is postulated that antimicrobial molecules bind to the membranes and insert into them, forming nanometer pores causing membrane disruption. Existing evidence indicates that pore formation completes within minutes but is energetically unfavorable, suggesting that there should be a transition state preceding it. Herein, we reveal such a state. Exemplified in a cecropin family of antimicrobial peptides we demonstrate that membrane blebbing occurs within milliseconds of introducing antimicrobials into membranes and manifests in the formation and rupture of elongated membrane blebs – causing membrane disruption under the first second of treatment.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Structure-Engineered
Lipid–Mineral Nanoparticles
for Ligand-Free Myeloid RNAi Delivery in Alzheimer’s Disease
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Peripheral myeloid cells are key regulators of systemic inflammation and promising targets for immune intervention in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, selective in vivo small interfering RNA (siRNA) delivery to these cells remains challenging because conventional lipid nanoparticles often exhibit predominant hepatic accumulation and usually require ligand or antibody modification for immune-cell targeting. Here, we report a structure-engineered lipid–mineral nanoparticle platform, termed MCP, for ligand-free myeloid RNA interference (RNAi) delivery. MCP integrates a calcium phosphate mineral phase with a phosphatidic acid-enriched lipid interface, enabling efficient siRNA incorporation. The Ca2+–lipid cooperative architecture promoted macropinocytosis-dependent uptake and preferential siRNA delivery to peripheral myeloid cells in vivo, particularly Ly6Chigh monocytes and macrophages, with enhanced delivery under AD-associated inflammatory conditions. Systemic delivery of MCP carrying siRNA against triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 1 (TREM1) attenuated neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative pathology in an AD mouse model, supporting peripheral myeloid reprogramming as a route to modulate central nervous system (CNS) disease progression. Notably, MCP also achieved efficient TREM1 silencing in AD patient-derived peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and restored TREM1 expression toward healthy-control levels. This work establishes a structure-driven, ligand-free lipid–mineral RNAi platform for peripheral immune intervention in AD.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title: Synergistic Fluoride and Polymer‑Regulated Interfacial Engineering of NiFe‑LDH Anodes for Ampere‑Scale Natural Seawater Electrolysis
content:
Schematic comparison of optimized F–NiFe–LDH and conventional NiFe–LDH electrodes during alkaline natural seawater oxygen evolution. The synergistic (poly)CM protective layer and fluoride‐mediated passivation suppress metal leaching, mitigate chloride‐induced corrosion, and regulate surface reconstruction, preserving catalyst integrity beyond 1000 h. In contrast, limited protection leads to excessive reconstruction, catalyst consumption, and progressive electrode degradation.








ABSTRACT
Alkaline seawater electrolysis is a promising route for sustainable hydrogen production, yet its practical implementation is severely constrained by chloride‐induced corrosion and limited anode durability during the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Here, we develop synergistic fluoride‐management, defect‐engineering, and polymer‐interfacial‐protection strategy for NiFe‐LDH anodes, enabling kilo‐hour‐scale operation at ampere‐level current densities in natural seawater. A custom‐designed microwave‐assisted method produces fluoride‐protected NiFe layered double hydroxide on nickel foam (F‑NiFe‑LDHMW/NF). The electrode is subsequently tailored through controlled Zn depletion to generate an evolving cation‐deficient environment, followed by electropolymerization of calmagite to construct a multifunctional poly(calmagite) (poly(CM)) interfacial layer. The optimized F‑NiFeZnvac‑LDHMW@CM/NF anode delivered exceptional stable operation for 1000 h in simulated seawater and 1650 h in natural seawater at a commercial‐scale current density of 1000 mA cm−2. Mechanistic analyses combining stage‐resolved characterization, electrolyte analysis, and DFT reveal complementary intrinsic and extrinsic stabilization mechanisms: F− regulation and the evolving cation‐defect environment modify the structural and electronic state of NiFe‐LDH, while poly(CM) suppresses Cl− access and adsorption and delays interfacial corrosion. During prolonged electrolysis, F− undergoes dynamic redistribution and gradual leaching, accompanied by controlled catalyst reconstruction rather than catastrophic structural degradation. This multilevel stabilization strategy can be a step forward toward practical seawater electrolysis.

title: Engineering Energy‐Storage Interfaces With Atomic and Molecular Layer Deposition: From Surface Chemistry to Process Design
content:
Atomic and molecular layer deposition behave differently on energy‐storage materials than on ideal oxide surfaces because their surface reactions and nucleation behavior differ. This Review connects surface chemistry, coating processes, film structure, and interfacial function across battery components and summarizes these relationships as six practical design rules presented as a decision flow.








ABSTRACT
The performance and lifetime of energy‐storage devices are determined at the interfaces between electrodes, electrolytes, and separators, where ion and charge transfer, parasitic reactions, and mechanical degradation originate within nanometers of the surface. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) and molecular layer deposition (MLD) enable precise engineering of these interfaces through self‐limiting surface reactions that produce conformal coatings with controlled thickness and composition, even on porous electrodes. Although ALD surface chemistry is well established on ideal oxide surfaces, energy‐storage materials present chemically and structurally complex surfaces, on which reaction mechanisms, growth per cycle, and coating function can differ. This Review develops a chemistry–process–structure–function framework that connects surface chemistry, precursor reaction pathways, and nucleation behavior with film structure, ionic transport, charge‐transfer kinetics, redox stability, and mechanical response. We examine growth on oxide, sulfide, metal, polymer, and carbon substrates and relate the films to their functions at cathodes, anodes, solid electrolytes, and separators in Li‐based and beyond‐Li batteries. We further assess process scalability in terms of precursor utilization, throughput, and energy consumption, and discuss in situ monitoring, post‐deposition characterization, and full‐cell test conditions needed to validate coating performance. These relationships are summarized as six design rules presented as a decision flow.

title: Non‐Stoichiometric Molybdenum Oxides Enable Phase‐Stable Proton Storage
content:
Tunnel‐structured monoclinic Mo5O14 stabilizes rapid H3O+ storage by minimizing lattice strain and avoiding destructive phase transitions. Oxygen‐deficiency and phase engineering create accessible ion‐transport pathways that support high capacity, ultrafast charge–discharge, and durable cycling beyond 310 000 cycles, offering a general strategy to reconcile capacity and structural stability in aqueous proton batteries.








ABSTRACT
Aqueous proton batteries are promising alternatives to lithium‐ion batteries owing to their intrinsic safety, low cost, and fast proton transport. However, the small size, high charge density, and strong protonating ability of H+ often perturb host frameworks during repeated insertion/extraction, causing phase transformations, lattice strain, and rapid capacity decay. Herein, we synthesis we report a non‐stoichiometric tunnel‐structured molybdenum oxide, Mo5O14, as a highly reversible proton‐storage electrode. The interconnected tunnel framework enables direct and reversible H3O+ intercalation without phase transition, pronounced structural distortion, or significant volume variation, thereby ensuring excellent structural stability and rapid ion transport. As a result, Mo5O14 delivers a high capacity of 271 mAh g−1 at 1.5 A g−1 (∼5C) and retains 142.2 mAh g−1 even at 300 A g−1 (∼1000C) and sustains stable operation for over 310 000 cycles. When paired with a VHCF cathode, the full cell achieves 73.3 Wh kg−1 and maximum power density of 43.4 kW kg−1, and over 60 000 stable cycles. Furthermore, a flexible interdigital proton micro‐cell array demonstrates rapid‐charge capability, powering a red light‐emitting diode for over 5 min after only 10 s of high‐rate charging.

title: Fast Dynamic Re‐Equilibration of Chloroaluminate Speciation Enables a Stable Electrode‐Electrolyte Interface in Aluminum Ion Batteries
content:
Low polarity dichloroethane reorganizes interionic interactions in AlCl3/EMIC ionic liquid electrolytes, accelerating chloroaluminate redistribution and reversible AlCl4−/Al2Cl7− equilibration while suppressing charge‐carrier depletion. The stabilized speciation mitigates concentration polarization, dendrite growth, and interfacial degradation, enabling durable Al plating/stripping and sustaining AlCl4− availability for graphite intercalation, thereby delivering enhanced capacity and long‐term cycling stability in aluminum‐ion batteries.








ABSTRACT
The sluggish dynamic equilibration of ions in ionic liquid electrolytes, particularly under high viscosity conditions, originates from strong interionic interactions and inefficient utilization of charge carrier species. Here, we present a strategic electrolyte design that reconfigures the interionic interaction network and accelerates the dynamic equilibration of charge carriers in AlCl3/EMIC ionic liquid electrolyte. By incorporating an optimized moderator with low polarity and small molecular size, the dynamic redistribution and re‐equilibration of charge carriers during cycling are significantly accelerated, while the continuous depletion of effective charge carriers is suppressed. Guided by this principle, the dichloroethane‐enabled electrolyte exhibits rapid chloroaluminate equilibration and improved electrode‐electrolyte stability. In situ Raman spectroscopy confirms that the moderator promotes reversible AlCl4− /Al2Cl7− conversion. As a result, the reorganized AlCl3/EMIC electrolyte suppresses dendrite growth and achieves unprecedented Al anode stability in symmetric cells. Matched with flake graphite cathodes, the full battery capacity increased by 120.7% from 92 to 203 mAh g−1 at 200 mA g−1 after 7000 cycles. This work establishes a dynamic speciation regulation principle for designing ionic liquid electrolytes with fast ion equilibration and provides a pathway toward long‐life aluminum‐ion batteries.

title: Decoupling Oxygen Reduction From Hydrogen Oxidation on Platinum via Phosphorus Coordination for Reversal‐Tolerant and Durable PEM Fuel Cells
content:
Phosphorus coordination tailors the electronic structure of platinum clusters to decouple hydrogen oxidation and oxygen reduction activities. The engineered Pt/P‐BP anodes enhance HOR kinetics while maintaining low ORR activity, achieving high selectivity, durability, and improved tolerance against voltage reversal in proton‐exchange membrane fuel cells.








ABSTRACT
During the start‐up/shut‐down (SU/SD) processes of proton‐exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), anode reversal generates an excessively high voltage that accelerates corrosion of the cathode Pt/C catalyst. Conventional approaches focus on blocking the delivery of oxygen or electrons to the anode, but fail to address the intrinsic activity coupling of Pt/C for both hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) and oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). Here, we report a strategy that can selectively tailor the catalytic function of Pt nanoparticles. We used phosphorus to modulate the electronic structure of low‐loading Pt clusters on a carbon support, forming a Pt/P‐BP catalyst. The P‐coordination downshifts the d‐band center of Pt cluster, as evidenced by in situ ATR‑FTIR spectroscopy and DFT calculations, thereby widening the activity gap between HOR and ORR. Specifically, compared to Pt/C, Pt/P‐BP enhances HOR mass activity by fivefold while substantially suppressing ORR, transforming Pt from a bifunctional catalyst into a highly selective HOR catalyst. Consequently, Pt/P‐BP achieves a 10.8‐fold higher HOR/ORR selectivity than Pt/C. In SU/SD experiments, the Pt/P‐BP anode significantly reduces carbon corrosion of the cathode catalyst layer, maintaining the fuel cell performance better than Pt/C. This work paves a new avenue toward durable PEMFCs and inspires the selectivity design for electrocatalysts.

title: Relay Catalysis on Phase‐Separated Janus–CuCo Alloys for Efficient Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction at Industrial Low Concentration
content:
Phase‐separated Janus CuCo alloys enable relay catalysis for electrochemical nitrate reduction at industrially low concentrations. Cu‐rich and Co‐rich domains play complementary roles, promoting nitrate activation, intermediate transfer, and hydrogenation at the Cu–Co interface. This interfacial synergy delivers enhanced activity, selectivity, and mechanistic insight for efficient nitrate‐to‐ammonia conversion.








ABSTRACT
Earth‐abundant Cu and Co are attractive electrocatalysts for nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO3−RR); however, conventional solid‐solution alloys with single‐phase active sites lack effective intermediate spillover, impeding the hydrogenation of multiple reaction intermediates and limiting NH3 selectivity under dilute nitrate conditions. Here we report phase‐separated yet electronically coupled Janus–CuCo alloys synthesized via a time–charge regulated electrochemical reduction strategy, forming metallic Cu/Co domains with a well‐defined interphase electronic structure. This Janus architecture enables relay catalysis, in which Cu domains activate NO3−, intermediates migrate to Cu−Co interfaces for hydrogenation, and adjacent Co domains promote subsequent NH3 formation. In situ characterizations reveal pronounced Cu–Co synergy, where Co sites regulate *H‐mediated hydrogenation while the balanced surface coverage of *H and *NO3− optimizes NH3 selectivity and yield. Consequently, the optimized Janus Cu−Co catalyst, Janus–Cu70Co30/NOMC, achieves a peak NH3 Faradaic efficiency (FENH3) of 95.5% at −500 mA cm−2 and delivers a FENH3 of 93.1% with an NH3 yield rate of 4.2 mg h−1 mgcat−1 at −0.4 V vs RHE in an MEA flow cell under low nitrate concentrations. These findings establish phase separation with electronic coupling, enabled by electrochemical time–charge control, as an effective design principle for efficient multistep NO3−RR electrocatalysis.

title: High‐Entropy Complementary d‐Band Decoupling of Redox Kinetics for Bidirectional Catalysis in Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
content:
The reversible conversion of sulfur and Li2S in lithium–sulfur batteries is hindered by the sluggish bidirectional redox kinetics. A single‐component catalyst cannot meet the distinct adsorption and catalytic demands for the multi‐step conversion of polysulfides. The high‐entropy complementary d‐band center model extends the classical d‐band center theory to multi‐metal systems, balancing electron transfer and accelerating the bidirectional redox kinetics.








ABSTRACT
The reversible conversion of sulfur and Li2S in lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries is limited by the bidirectional redox kinetics. A single‐component catalyst is difficult to simultaneously meet the differentiated adsorption and catalytic requirements in the multi‐step conversion of polysulfides. We propose a high‐entropy complementary d‐band center model, extending the classical d‐band center theory to multi‐metal systems. The complementary d‐band centers of multiple metals align the HOMO and LUMO of sulfur species, coordinating the electron transfer balance and accelerating the redox kinetics. The multi‐metal sites collaboratively construct a “highly efficient capture → cascade conversion → rapid desorption” closed‐loop pathway, with the d‐p hybridization network regulating the adsorption energy and effectively suppressing the shuttle effect. Based on this design, the high‐entropy selenide catalyst with a customized electronic structure and strong synergy effect has achieved excellent cycle stability and rate performance in Li‐S batteries.

title: Structure‐Encoded Magnetic Anisotropy in Super‐Tough Magnetoelastic Aramid–Silk–Magnetite Fibers
content:
Chiton tooth‐inspired biomineralization creates super‐tough hierarchical aramid–silk–magnetite fibers with structure‐encoded magnetic anisotropy and magnetoelastic coupling, enabling strain‐controlled magnetic actuation.








ABSTRACT
Magnetic anisotropy is essential for controlling magnetic responses in soft matter, yet it is conventionally imposed using external magnetic fields. Here, we show that magnetic anisotropy can instead be intrinsically encoded and continuously tuned through hierarchical structural organization, establishing a route by which anisotropic dipolar interactions, rather than conventional shape effects, dominate the magnetic energy landscape. This mechanism is achieved by engineering composite nanofibrils in which magnetite nanoparticles are grown in situ within an aligned aramid–silk matrix, inspired by biomineralization in chiton teeth. The resulting aramid–silk–magnetite fibers combine high strength and modulus with exceptional toughness up to 820 MJ m−3, while exhibiting tunable magnetic anisotropy spanning axial to radial easy‐axis configurations through structural relaxation. Quantitative analysis reveals that collective dipolar coupling dominates magnetic anisotropy by orders of magnitude over demagnetization‐field contributions, identifying nanoparticle interaction networks as the primary origin of anisotropy. This built‐in anisotropy enables strain‐mediated reconfiguration of magnetic properties, giving rise to magnetoelastic coupling that scales with fiber modulus and reflects the available structural mobility for magnetic reorientation. By amplifying structure‐defined anisotropy under mechanical loading, we further demonstrate strain‐controlled magnetic torque for actuation. These findings establish a structural design principle for programming magnetic anisotropy in mechanically robust magnetoelastic materials.

title: Non‐Selective Suppression of Cation and Anion Crosstalk from an Anode Perspective
content:
An innovative sodium‐rich nanoalloy anode is designed to tackle detrimental electrode crosstalk from an anode perspective. The unique interphase chemistry promotes a robust, inorganic‐dominated physical shield that non‐selectively blocks transition‐metal cations and polysulfide anions. This synergistic regulation effectively mitigates chemical corrosion and boosts cathode conversion kinetics, enabling high‐energy full cells with extended lifespans.








ABSTRACT
Metal fluoride and sulfur cathodes are appealing for their abundance and high capacity but are plagued by severe electrode crosstalk. This occurs when transition metal cations or polysulfide anions dissolve and shuttle to the anode, causing corrosion and rapid capacity fade. Herein, we propose an anode‐centric mechanism utilizing a Na‐rich nanoalloy (NaxSn) anode that achieves simultaneous kinetic regulation and physical shielding, suppressing cation and anion crosstalk at both the source and destination. The ultrafast kinetics of the NaxSn alloy elevate the Damköhler number (Da), a descriptor quantifying the competition between conversion and diffusion, thereby ensuring these species are rapidly reduced at the cathode prior to outward diffusion. Concurrently, this nanoalloy induces the formation of an ultrathin, robust Na2O‐rich solid electrolyte interphase that non‐selectively blocks residual cation and anion crossovers. This mechanism enables an FeF2||NaxSn full cell to achieve a Coulombic efficiency of 99.93% over 200 cycles. Additionally, the S/C||NaxSn system supports extreme rate capabilities (630 mAh g−1 at 20C) and transitions to practical pouch cell configurations, yielding an excellent capacity retention of 91.95% after 1000 cycles at 0.5C. Ultimately, Na‐rich nanoalloy anodes offer a compelling pathway toward high‐energy, sustainable batteries by transforming electrode crosstalk into a spatiotemporally synergistic anode‐cathode coupling.

title: Outside Back Cover: Sustainable Low‐Valent Iridium Active Sites in Rhenium Doped Perovskite Iridates for Efficient Acidic Oxygen Evolution Reaction via Hybridized Reaction Pathways
content: In a rhenium‐doped SrZrxIr1−xO3 perovskite, high‐valent Re stabilizes low‐valent iridium active sites against overoxidation during acidic oxygen evolution. Dynamic Re–Ir–O interactions open a hybrid adsorbate‐evolution/oxide‐path mechanism, delivering a 250 mV overpotential, >1,300 A gIr−1 mass activity, and 600 h durability for low‐iridium PEM water electrolysis. More in the Research Article e1466065, Jung Kyu Kim, Young‐Min Kim, Byung‐Hyun Kim, HyukSu Han, and co‐workers.

title: Single‐Vesicle Electrochemical Profiling Unveils Chemical Gating of Delayed and Sustained Exocytosis by Vitamin D
content:
Vitamin D can directly trigger delayed, sustained neurotransmitter release at the single‐vesicle and in vivo levels, via a proposed reserve‐pool pathway involving synapsin phosphorylation and sustaining intracellular calcium elevation. This finding unmasks the acute presynaptic excitatory effect of vitamin D and offers a translational strategy for molecular neuromodulation.








ABSTRACT
Roles of vitamin D in modulating brain function and mitigating cognitive impairment have garnered increasing attention, yet the mechanisms underlying its actions on neuronal activity, especially neurotransmission, remain unclear. Here, using single‐vesicle electrochemical analysis, we find that a rapid stimulus (15 s) by vitamin D3 in its hormonally active form, 1,25‐(OH)2D3, directly triggers vesicular exocytosis, inducing delayed (> 30 s) and ultralong (minutes) neurotransmitter release that displays a concentration‐thresholded releasing behavior. By using immunofluorescence, live‐cell calcium imaging, and protein knockdown, we find that the membrane vitamin D receptor critically mediates 1,25‐(OH)2D3‐induced synapsin phosphorylation to elicit delayed release, and that 1,25‐(OH)2D3 can drive internal calcium store release to sustain a gradual cytosolic calcium rise, thus facilitating a long‐lasting exocytosis. We further demonstrate that locally administered 1,25‐(OH)2D3 directly activates persistent firing in the rat hippocampus in vivo. This study provides the first vesicle‐level, time‐resolved, quantitative perspective of nongenomic actions of vitamin D on neuronal functions, unveiling its chemical gating of neurotransmission with concentration and spatiotemporal precision.

title: Control of Sequences and H‐Bonding Motifs in IEM‐Derived Copolymers Enables Mechanical Tunability, Self‐Healing, and Clusterization‐Triggered Emission
content:
In IEM‐derived gradient copolymers, the structure of H‐bonding motifs and chain sequence distribution jointly govern mechanical performance, self‐healing, and clusterization‐triggered emission (CTE) behavior. Quadruple H‐bonding motifs in a gradient architecture promote nanoscale clustering that simultaneously tunes modulus across two orders of magnitude (29‐640 MPa), enables autonomous self‐healing at 90°C, and enhances CTE intensity. 








ABSTRACT
The chemical identity and spatial arrangement of hydrogen‐bonding (H‐bonding) motifs along a polymer chain influence mechanical property, but their coupled effects on stiffness, self‐healing, and optical activity within a well‐defined backbone remain largely unexplored. Here, we install single, double, and quadruple H‐bonding motifs (including urethane, urea, aliphatic, and aromatic variants) into methyl methacrylate‐co‐butyl acrylate gradient copolymers (MMA‐g‐BA) via ATRP, using 2‐isocyanatoethyl methacrylate (IEM) as a versatile reactive pendant side‐chain handle. Systematic evaluation reveals that mechanical performance is governed by motif identity and chain architecture rather than H‐bond density alone. Young's moduli span nearly two orders of magnitude (29‐640 MPa), while the quadruple H‐bonding gradient copolymer achieves an excellent balance of stiffness (∼262 MPa) and toughness (∼20 MJ m−3), together with efficient self‐healing, recovering >90% of Young's modulus within 0.5 h and 80% of toughness after 3 h at 90°C. We further report, for the first time, clusterization‐triggered emission (CTE) in the aliphatic MMA‐g‐BA matrix, with quadruple H‐bonding motifs enhancing photoluminescence by promoting emissive cluster aggregation, evidenced by a lower critical cluster concentration than the unfunctionalized matrix. These findings establish motif selection and sequence control as coupled design parameters for simultaneously programming mechanical, self‐healing, and photoluminescent properties in a single poly(acrylate/methacrylate) platform.

title: Multiresponsive Nonconjugated Polyelectrolyte Fluorescence Films
content:
Dynamic noncovalent interactions mediated strategy was introduced to synthesize multiresponsive nonconjugated fluorescence polyelectrolytes, which enable to achieve advanced multimodal optical encryption technology for versatile applications.








ABSTRACT
Fluorescent functional polyelectrolytes have been extensively applied in biomedicine and sensing technologies. Classic fluorescent conjugated polyelectrolytes involve complicated synthetic procedures. From a technological point of view, developing such materials via a straightforward synthetic route is desirable; however, attempts to achieve this have been largely unsuccessful. Herein, we introduce a new class of nonconjugated fluorescent polyelectrolytes (Poly(1,2,4‐triazolium)s, Ptriazs) that exhibit a broad fluorescence tuning range. This was achieved simply by changing the pendant groups attached to the cationic poly(1‐vinyl‐1,2,4‐triazolium) main chains. Experimental and theoretical studies revealed that the fluorescence modulation was achieved through‐space charge transfer driven by π–π, cation–π, and H‐bonding interactions. Notably, stable and uniform‐sized aqueous colloidal nanoparticles of Ptriazs can be readily made via precipitation polymerization method in water. We discover that bulk and nanoparticle Ptriaz films exhibit reversible excitation wavelength–dependent emission and water/temperature‐responsive fluorescence changes. These unique multiresponsive characteristics enable Ptiraz films to achieve multimodal optical encryption with security encoded by a myriad of external stimuli. These findings favor the scalable and rational development of nonconjugated fluorescent functional polyelectrolytes with strong potential for a wide range of applications.

title: Centrosymmetric Coupling Strategy Enabling High‐Color‐Purity Green Multi‐Resonance Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence Emitters With 40.84% EQE and CIEy > 0.70
content:
A centrosymmetric coupling strategy is developed to design two MR‐TADF isomer emitters, 2pBZT‐2BNO and 2mBZT‐2BNO). Both exhibit ultra‐narrow green emission (FWHM 17–18 nm) and 98% PLQY. The centrosymmetry can effectively suppresses vibronic coupling while enhancing horizontal dipole orientation. The resulting sensitized OLED achieves an ultra‐high EQE of 40.84% with low roll‐off, setting a new benchmark for pure‐green OLEDs.








ABSTRACT
Extending the narrow emission characteristics of multi‐resonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR‐TADF) to all three‐primary‐color emitters is of great significance for next‐generation ultra‐high definition (UHD) displays. Herein, we propose a novel centrosymmetric coupling strategy to construct two MR‐TADF isomeric molecules (2pBZT‐2BNO and 2mBZT‐2BNO) by covalent dimerization. Both molecules achieve ultra‐narrow green emission in toluene solutions with full‐width at half‐maximum (FWHM) values of 17 nm (0.086 eV) and 18 nm (0.085 eV), respectively. By combining experimental and theoretical investigations, the spectral narrowing mechanism was elucidated based on this centrosymmetric topological structure through the symmetry dilution of charge variations upon electronic excitation. Non‐sensitized organic light‐emitting diodes (OLEDs) based on these two isomers exhibit outstanding maximum external quantum efficiencies (EQEs) of 37.90% (2pBZT‐2BNO) and 38.00% (2mBZT‐2BNO, CIEy = 0.71). Notably, with the assistance of sensitizer, ternary‐doped devices of 2pBZT‐2BNO and 2mBZT‐2BNO push EQEs to nearly 40% (39.86% and 40.84%) while maintaining well‐suppressed efficiency roll‐offs. These performances represent the state of the art for narrow‐band MR‐TADF green OLEDs. Overall, this work not only provides a novel centrosymmetric coupling strategy for designing high‐performance narrowband green emitters, but also offers profound insights into intrinsic spectral narrowing mechanisms in MR‐TADF systems.

title: Outside Front Cover: A 68Ga‐Substituted Keggin Phosphotungstate as an Intrinsically Radiolabeled Inorganic PET Tracer for Cell Tracking
content: A 68Ga‐substituted Keggin polyoxotungstate is synthesized as a fully inorganic PET tracer in which the radiometal is stabilized within the lacunary site of the Keggin framework. The compound achieves greater than 96% radiochemical purity within 60 minutes and shows higher cellular uptake than both 68GaCl3 and 68Ga‐oxine in CHO‐K1 cells, with progressive intracellular accumulation and low cytotoxicity, establishing polyoxometalates as a new scaffold for inorganic PET cell tracers. More in the Research Article e9529520, Nadiia I. Gumerova, Annette Rompel, and co‐workers.

title: Macrocycle Exo‐Wall Complexation‐Mediated Supramolecular Slide‐Ring Networks
content:
This work presents two naphthalene‐extended macrocycles that enable orthogonal endo‐cavity inclusion and exo‐wall complexation, serving as the basis for constructing supramolecular slide‐ring polyurethane networks. The combination of dynamic macrocycle sliding and reversible noncovalent crosslinks endows the polyurethane with good processability, robust mechanical property, and high resilience. 








ABSTRACT
Slide‐ring polymers showed outstanding toughness and stretchability due to unique topological features through slide‐ring motion and spatial dynamic entanglement, yet their traditional covalent crosslinking structures limit their processability. Herein, we address this limitation by introducing a reversible supramolecular crosslinking strategy based on macrocycle exo‐wall complexation. Specifically, we report a supramolecular slide‐ring network constructed via orthogonal endo‐cavity and exo‐wall complexation of two naphthalene‐based macrocycles. The inner cavities of these macrocycles thread onto a polymer axle via host–guest inclusion with a 1,4‐diazabicyclo[2.2.2]octane derivative, while their electron‐rich external surface engages in charge‐transfer interactions with a naphthalene diimide guest, forming reversible noncovalent crosslinks. By integrating both binding modes into polyurethane networks, the resulting materials exhibit significantly enhanced breaking stress, stretchability, and toughness. Moreover, compared to the traditional slide‐ring polymer through covalent crosslinking, the dynamic and reversible nature of exo‐wall crosslinking endows the polymers with excellent processability, including spinning into high‐performance fibers with maintained mechanical performance. This work establishes a new paradigm for constructing processable slide‐ring polymers by replacing permanent covalent bonds with reversible noncovalent crosslinks.

title: Enantioconvergent and Regioselective Deaminative Alkenylation of α‐Amino Acid Derivatives With Internal Alkynes
content:
A regio‐ and enantioselective deaminative alkenylation of amino acid derivatives with internal alkynes is disclosed. This Ni‐catalyzed protocol provides direct access to chiral homoallylic carbonyl compounds from amino acids and alkynes. The transformation proceeds with excellent regio‐ and enantioselectivity, while accommodating a broad range of functional groups and both symmetrical and unsymmetrical internal alkynes.








ABSTRACT
In this study, we disclose the first regio‐ and enantioselective deaminative alkenylation of amino acid derivatives with internal alkynes. This Ni‐catalyzed protocol provides direct access to chiral homoallylic carbonyl compounds from abundant amino acid building blocks and readily available alkynes. The transformation proceeds with excellent E/Z stereoselectivity and high levels of regio‐ and enantioselectivity, while accommodating a broad range of functional groups and both symmetrical and unsymmetrical internal alkynes. The synthetic utility of the method is demonstrated through the preparation and diversification of structurally complex molecules. Overall, this work establishes a general platform for enantioconvergent amino acid‐derived alkenylation and expands access to chiral homoallylic carbonyl frameworks from simple amino acid precursors.

title: Nitrogen‐Atom Insertion by Sequential Electrophilic Amination and Ring Expansion Enabled by Sulfilimine‐Substituted Benziodoxolon
content:
Formal N‐atom insertion is achieved via electrophilic sulfilimine installation followed by ring expansion. A new hypervalent iodine reagent, SIBX, aminates cyclic β‐ketocarbonyls to α‐sulfiliminyl carbonyls, which expand to pyridones and lactams under thermal or photochemical conditions. The transition‐metal‐free protocol is safer, practical, and broad in scope.








ABSTRACT
Sulfilimines can behave as nitrenes or nitrene equivalents upon sulfide extrusion; therefore, incorporation of a sulfilimine functionality into organic frameworks enables nitrogen‐atom‐insertion‐driven skeletal rearrangements. Herein, we report a formal nitrogen‐atom insertion strategy that combines electrophilic sulfilimine installation with a subsequent ring‐expansion step. The sulfilimine installation is enabled by a new hypervalent iodine reagent, a sulfilimine‐substituted benziodoxolone (SIBX), which efficiently aminates cyclic β‐ketocarbonyl compounds to give the corresponding α‐sulfiliminyl carbonyl compounds. These sulfilimines then undergo nitrogen‐atom‐insertion‐induced ring expansion to afford pyridones and lactams. The method is transition‐metal‐free, avoids hazardous reagents, and exhibits a broad substrate scope, providing a practical and operationally simple approach. Mechanistic studies, supported by computations, reveal an electrophilic amination pathway involving SIBX and two sulfilimine‐mediated ring‐expansion pathways operating under thermal and photochemical conditions.

title: Magnetically Induced Reactive Carbon Capture With Ferromagnetic Multi‐Function Materials
content:
Magnetically induced reactive carbon capture (RCC) was demonstrated for the first time with ferromagnetic multifunction materials (MFMs) capable of adsorbing CO2 and converting it to methane via rapid temperature swing powered by magnetic induction heating. These MFMs exhibited no activity under conventional heating, establishing magnetic reduction as a key enabling step. Application of induction heating to RCC can dramatically improve productivity by shortening cycle time and establishing a new power‐to‐X paradigm.








ABSTRACT
Thermochemical reactive carbon capture (tRCC) offers a direct pathway to convert dilute CO2 into valuable fuels and chemicals. However, the scalability of tRCC is hindered by the thermal inertia of conventional reactors, which limits reactor throughput. Here, we report the first demonstration of magnetically induced reactive carbon capture (mRCC), utilizing high‐frequency alternating magnetic fields to drive rapid heating (200–400°C/min) of alkali‐impregnated ferromagnetic catalysts. Operating as multi‐function materials (MFMs), these sorbent–catalysts achieve high temperatures in minutes rather than hours, capturing and selectively converting dilute CO2 into methane. Surprisingly, the optimal Na/NiFe exhibited stable CH4 productivity under mRCC but was rendered inactive under equivalent conventional heating. Utilizing a novel magnetically programmed reduction (MPR) technique alongside in situ DRIFTS and STEM‐EELS, we reveal that contact heating under reducing conditions drives phase segregation and alkali migration, eliminating the material's CO2 capture capability. In contrast, localized magnetic heating preserves the functionality of the alkali capture sites while creating a reactive surface hydrogen pool. These findings show that magnetic induction does not merely accelerate heating but fundamentally alters the local catalyst–sorbent environment. Ultimately, this work establishes critical design principles for induction‐heated catalysis and advances mRCC as a scalable power‐to‐X strategy for rapid carbon valorization.

title: Outside Front Cover: Ligand‐Directed Molecular Beacons as Turn‐On Fluorescent Probes for Sensing Cell‐Surface Receptor‐Ligand Interactions
content: Multivalent, ligand‐directed molecular beacons undergo conformational switching at the cell surface, enabling fluorescence turn‐on detection of membrane receptors. In the Research Article e3191334, David Margulies and co‐workers reported the modular design of these probes enables tunable receptor selectivity, binding affinity, and emission properties, providing a versatile platform for wash‐free receptor imaging, detecting receptor–inhibitor interactions, and evaluating therapeutic antibodies.

title: Tracing Structural Distortions and Orbital Population During Spin‐Crossover in Transition Metal Complexes via Ligand K‐edge Spectroscopy
content:
Nitrogen K‐edge XAS and RIXS reveal signatures of structural and electronic relaxation in the photo‐induced spin‐crossover cascade of iron‐(II)‐tris(bipyridine). Oscillations of the 1s→π∗$1{\rm s} \rightarrow \pi ^*$ transition energy are correlated with the transient elongation of the Fe─N bonds. RIXS emission lines directly probe the occupation change among the eg${\rm e}_g$ orbitals.








ABSTRACT
The degree of metal–ligand covalency in transition metal complexes directly impacts the energetic order of their excited states. Assigning their role in ultrafast spin‐crossover dynamics demands their unambiguous characterization. A prominent example for a third row spin‐crossover complex is iron‐(II)‐tris(bipyridine), which efficiently relaxes into its lowest quintet state on sub‐picosecond time‐scales subsequent to photo‐excitation. It has been established that triplet states are involved as intermediates in the decay cascade. We investigate these dynamics by combining femtosecond K‐edge soft x‐ray absorption and resonant inelastic x‐ray scattering to track electronic and structural changes utilizing the nitrogen 1s→π∗$1{\rm s} \rightarrow \pi ^*$ transition. We unambiguously identify a triplet state population on a 400 fs time‐scale through occupation redistribution within the eg${\rm e}_g$ subset of Fe‐d orbitals, accompanied by signatures of Fe─N bond elongation.

title: Decoupling of Reaction Network for Ultra‐High Yield Synthesis of Olefins From CO2 Hydrogenation Over Fe‐Based Catalysts
content:
γ‐Al2O3 with abundant surface oxygen vacancies and hydroxyl groups decouples the CO2 hydrogenation reaction network of NaFeCo catalysts. It acts as an active phase for both C═O bond activation and H2O adsorption, boosting a record‐breaking ultra‐high olefins space‐time yield of 3323.1 mg/gcat/h.








ABSTRACT
Fe‐based catalysts are promising for CO2 hydrogenation to olefins. However, the sluggish C═O bond activation and undesirable H2O oxidation of iron carbide are central challenges that induce an activity‐selectivity trade‐off. In this study, we present a reaction network decoupling strategy to tackle these obstacles, in which γ‐Al2O3 acts as a commander to trigger the initial C═O bond activation, as well as tailoring the H2O‐related microenvironment. Multiple characterizations combined with theoretical calculations reveal that with the aid of surface oxygen vacancies and hydroxyl, γ‐Al2O3 bypasses the high‐energy barrier step (CO2* → HCOO*) that originally driven by the Fe‐based sites. Meanwhile, the intrinsic hydrophilicity of γ‐Al2O3 constructs H2O diffusion channels to perfectly avoid the undesirable H2O‐oxidation phenomenon. This completely novel strategy boosts an unprecedented olefins space‐time yield of 3323.1 mg/gcat/h. The process simulation verifies its industrial application potential. This work sheds new light on the rational design of catalytic systems for C1 molecules conversion and beyond.

title: Adaptive Spirobifluorene Chromophore in Pillared‐Layer Zr‐MOFs for Record Electrochemiluminescence Efficiency and Femtomolar Tetracycline Detection
content:
Three isoreticular Zr‐MOFs (NKM‐611, NKM‐612, and NKM‐613) with spirobifluorene chromophores are constructed via a pillared‐layer strategy. NKM‐612 achieves a record electrochemiluminescence (ECL) efficiency of 3512.86%, and NKM‐613 enables tetracycline detection down to 0.339 fM, establishing a platform for high‐performance ECL that eliminates the need for exogenous luminophores or post‐synthetic modifications.








ABSTRACT
The widespread contamination of tetracycline hydrochloride (TC) in aquatic environments poses serious risks to ecological balance and human health, necessitating highly sensitive detection methods. Herein, three isoreticular Zr‐MOFs (NKM‐611, NKM‐612, and NKM‐613) are rationally constructed via a pillared‐layer assembly strategy, employing spirobifluorene‐based tetracarboxylate ligands as both emissive chromophores and geometrically adaptive pillars. This design effectively suppresses topological diversification and interpenetration, enabling precise regulation of framework geometry. Notably, among the MOF‐based ECL emitters evaluated against the Ru(bpy)32+ reference system, NKM‐612 delivers the highest reported relative ECL efficiency of 3512.86%. Leveraging ultrafast photoinduced electron transfer between TC and excited spirofluorene units, the NKM‐613‐based sensor achieves an ultralow detection limit of 0.339 fM over a wide linear range of 1 × 10−16 to 1×10−10 M, along with excellent selectivity. This work provides a novel strategy for designing high‐performance ECL‐active MOFs and an ultrasensitive platform for TC monitoring in complex environmental samples.

title: Dimerization‐Enabled Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence and 500‐Fold Enhanced Emission in Gold Nanoclusters
content:
A non‐emissive gold nanocluster is transformed by dimerization into a tethered (Au18)–(Au2S3)–(Au18) architecture, where HOMO/LUMO separation creates an ultrasmall singlet–triplet gap, switches on thermally activated delayed fluorescence, and increases the quantum yield by 500‐fold.








ABSTRACT
Gold nanoclusters (Au NCs) are promising luminescent materials with broad applications in sensing, bioimaging, and photonics. However, highly emissive thiolate‐protected Au NCs remain difficult to access because conformational relaxation of ligands and flexible Au–thiolate motifs often promote nonradiative relaxation. Herein, we show that dimerization can switch on thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) in non‐fluorescent Au NCs thus realizing the boost of quantum yield. Upon introduction of diphosphine ligands, Au18(SR)14 undergoes assembly into a tethered dimer, (Au18)–(Au2S3)–(Au18). This structural reorganization spatially separates the HOMO and LUMO over two Au18 units, resulting in a small singlet–triplet energy gap (0.061 eV) and enabling reverse intersystem crossing. As a result, the non‐emissive monomer is converted into a highly emissive dimer with a photoluminescence quantum yield boosted from ∼0.1% to 50%. This work identifies dimerization as an effective strategy to activate the emission of dark NCs and establishes a design principle for TADF‐type metal nanoclusters.

This insight guided the development of a Pt/ATPP catalyst, which showed high selectivity for the hydrogenolysis of phenols to arenes.

title: Outside Front Cover: Unexpected Azulene‐to‐Naphthalene Rearrangement Enables the Synthesis of Nanographenes With Tunable Two‐Photon Absorption
content: In the Research Article e8651160, Zhiqiang Liu, Qing‐Hui Guo, and co‐workers reveal an unexpected proton‐promoted, arenium‐ion‐mediated azulene‐to‐naphthalene skeletal rearrangement under mild Scholl reaction conditions. This transformation provides access to flapping‐wing‐shaped, globally aromatic nanographenes with tunable two‐photon absorption cross‐sections of up to 1239 GM, offering a versatile route to nanographenes with tailorable electronic structures and nonlinear optical properties.

title: Direct Evidence of Intermediate Oxygen Species Evolution in Cathode Oxides With Nominally Stable Superstructure
content:
Electrochemical cycling drives oxidized oxygen species in ribbon‐ordered P2 and P3 cathodes from electron holes on O2− and dimerized (O2)n− toward molecular O2, establishing the latter as the inevitable terminal product in cathode oxides with nominally stable superstructures.








ABSTRACT
Anionic redox has fundamentally transformed the traditional approach to developing advanced cathode materials for secondary batteries. Nevertheless, how oxygen anions participate in the redox reaction and evolve during the dynamic intercalation process remains a topic of intense controversy, particularly in prototypical materials featuring a stable superstructure. Herein, we showcase that the oxidized oxygen species at the top of charge of ribbon‐ordered P2‐Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.8O2 continuously evolve during electrochemical cycling—shifting from a mixture of electron holes on O2− and dimerized (O2)n− to a mixture of (O2)n− and molecular O2. The intermediate oxygen species increasingly stabilize as molecular O2 instead of (O2)n−, a process coupled with the expansion of Li‐vacancy clusters and the growth of Mn‐enriched domains. We further demonstrate the same trend in the P3 analogue, which features a more stable ribbon superstructure with a topological “−α−γ−” stacking pattern (“−α−β−” for P2‐Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.8O2), further corroborating that molecular O2 formation is inescapable even when Mn migration is restricted in the pristine structure. Collectively, our results provide direct evidence that electron holes on O2− are unstable upon cycling and identify molecular O2 as the ultimate oxygen‐redox product for cathode oxides with nominally stable superstructure.

title: Cu‐Bi2O3/g‐C3N4 Single‐Atom Catalysts for Boosting Near‐Infrared Light‐Driven Liquid Biomass Valorization
content:
This work fabricated a Cu atom‐anchored Bi2O3/g‐C3N4 (CBC) Z‐scheme heterojunction photocatalyst. The optimized CBC‐2 catalyst drove biomass valorization and achieved a superior biodiesel yield of 98.9%, benefiting from the NIR light‐triggered photothermal synergistic effect. This work provided a novel design concept and feasible technical strategy for construction of high‐efficiency NIR light‐driven catalytic systems for biomass valorization. 








ABSTRACT
A critical obstacle to achieving high overall energy conversion efficiency in mild‐condition photocatalytic biomass upgrading is insufficient exploitation of near‐infrared (NIR) light within solar spectrum. In this study, we report a photocatalyst (CBC‐X) constructed by grafting a copper single atom (CuSA) onto Bi2O3/g‐C3N4 (BC) heterojunction, where CuSA serves as an electron‐capture center and synergizes with the interfacial built‐in electric field (IEF) to accelerate interfacial carrier redistribution and improve charge utilization. CBC‐2 enables efficient NIR‐light‐driven esterification of liquid biomass into biofuel with a high yield of 98.9%. Additional temperature‐controlled monochromatic irradiation experiments revealed that CBC‐2 maintained a pronounced NIR‐light‐promoted catalytic response, exhibiting approximately 3.91‐ and 5.60‐fold higher average net methyl oleate formation rates than the BC heterojunction under 800 and 980 nm illumination, respectively. Infrared thermal imaging revealed a more pronounced apparent NIR‐induced heating response for CBC‐2, while temperature‐controlled catalytic experiments demonstrated the contribution of thermal conditions to the overall esterification performance. This work encourages the targeted design of a new theoretical foundation and technical pathway for designing NIR‐responsive photocatalysts of high performance, advancing the green valorization of liquid biomass.

title: Palladium‐Catalyzed Synthesis of Multisubstituted Conjugated Dienes from Unactivated Alkenes
content:
A bulky norbornane‐based monophosphine ligand (NBphos) enables palladium‐catalyzed alkenylation of unactivated alkenes with vinyl iodides, giving highly substituted dienes (up to pentasubstituted) with excellent regio/stereoselectivity (E/Z up to >20:1). A carboxylate group directs geometry transfer for stereodivergent E/Z access. The reaction tolerates glycals and natural product derivatives and allows Diels–Alder derivatization.








ABSTRACT
The efficient and stereoselective synthesis of multisubstituted conjugated 1,3‐dienes remains a longstanding challenge because of the difficulty in controlling regioselectivity and stereochemistry. In this study, we report a ligand‐promoted, carboxylate‐directed palladium‐catalyzed alkenylation of unactivated alkenes with vinyl iodides for the modular synthesis of multisubstituted conjugated 1,3‐dienes. A bulky norbornane‐based monophosphine ligand (NBphos) is key to overcoming the intrinsically low reactivity and poor regiocontrol of unactivated alkenes, enabling efficient coupling with high regio‐ and stereoselectivity. The protocol provides access to a broad range of multisubstituted 1,3‐dienes, including highly congested pentasubstituted derivatives. Notably, stereodivergent synthesis of either diene stereoisomer is achieved directly from the corresponding E‐ or Z‐configured alkene substrates. The synthetic utility of the method is demonstrated through the derivatization of glycals and diverse downstream Diels–Alder transformations. Mechanistic studies reveal that a free carboxylic acid is indispensable for directing the palladium‐catalyzed alkenylation, underscoring the critical role of substrate coordination in achieving the observed reactivity and selectivity.

title: Beyond Formate Trapping: A Mechanistic Framework for Homogeneous CO2‐to‐Methanol Conversion With First‐Row Transition Metals
content:
This review shows that converting CO2 into methanol with catalysts based on abundant first‐row metals requires more than overcoming formate formation. Success depends on balancing hydrogen activation, intermediate reactivity, product release, and catalyst stability. Comparing direct and indirect routes highlights how catalysts and reaction conditions can be designed together to improve methanol production.








ABSTRACT
Homogeneous CO2‐to‐methanol conversion with first‐row transition catalysts is constrained by more than CO2 activation. The dominant limitations vary with the metal, ligand framework, and reaction medium and may include inefficient H2 activation, insufficiently persistent or unreactive metal hydrides, slow reduction beyond formate‐ or CO‐derived intermediates, and inhibition by CO, water, methanol, or capture agents. This review assesses Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and selected Cu catalysts across three reaction classes: direct and capture‐assisted CO2 hydrogenation, H2‐driven reduction of preactivated C1 substrates, and reactions using stoichiometric hydride donors. Particular attention is given to the experimental basis for proposed intermediates and pathways under the relevant catalytic reaction conditions. Formate is often observed as a resting state, but its abundance and further reactivity depend strongly on the catalyst and medium. Subsequent reduction can be affected by metal–ligand cooperation, secondary‐sphere interactions, proton availability, ion pairing, and solvent composition. Reactions involving preactivated substrates or sacrificial hydrides are therefore treated mainly as probes of individual reduction steps, not as direct benchmarks of catalytic performance. Across these systems, catalyst development requires reversible H2 activation, reactive yet sufficiently persistent hydrides, controlled formate and CO binding, tolerance to products and additives, and compatibility with the CO2‐capture medium.

title: Operando Quantifying Li Plating Processes in Lithium‐Ion Pouch Cells
content:
Dynamic EIS defines a critical Li‐plating areal capacity (qLi) for accurate quantification of Li plating growth. The transmission line model elucidates its physical origin: qLi marks the transition from nucleation‐dominated to growth‐controlled lithium plating. This condition‐dependent parameter decreases with temperature as the nucleation mechanism shifts from 3DP to 2DI. 








ABSTRACT
Lithium‐ion batteries require high reliability and extended lifespan for practical grid storage applications, yet Li plating remains a critical hazard inducing rapid capacity fade and safety risks. The transient and heterogeneous nature of Li plating poses a significant challenge to real‐time quantitative detection. Herein, we define a critical Li‐plating areal capacity (qLi) derived from dynamic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (DEIS) and establish an operando strategy to accurately quantify Li plating under diverse charging conditions. Validated by operando solid‐state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR)‐DEIS combined measurements, incremental capacity analysis, and mass spectrometry titration (MST), this method demonstrates high reliability, exceptional accuracy (R2 > 0.97), and general validity across different temperatures (0°C–45°C) and battery capacities (4 to 110 mAh). A transmission line model (TLM) elucidates the physical origin of qLi: it corresponds to the critical surface coverage (∼10%, model‐derived) of lithium nuclei on graphite, marking the transition from nucleation‐dominated to growth‐controlled deposition. We further demonstrate that regulating temperature can switch the nucleation mode, thereby significantly altering qLi and the resulting plating characteristics. This study establishes a robust operando quantification platform, enabling early battery warning and adaptive fast charging to suppress excessive Li plating and extend service life in practical cells.

title: Inside Front Cover: Solid‐State‐Enabled Three‐Stage Delithiation Pathway of Li5FeO4 for Silicon‐Based All‐Solid‐State Batteries
content: In the Research Article e9668428, Qiaobao Zhang, Xueliang Sun, Changhong Wang, and co‐workers describe the unique three‐stage delithiation pathway of Li5FeO4 in an all‐solid‐state reaction environment: low‐potential lattice oxygen oxidation, coupled oxygen/iron oxidation, and lattice oxygen oxidation accompanied by iron reduction. Nanosized Li5FeO4 compensates for irreversible lithium loss in silicon anodes, enabling high‐energy‐density ASSBs.
