title: Atroposelective Access to Bicyclic Peptides via an Amide Photocaging Strategy
content:
Ansamers are an atypical class of atropisomers (Pansa/Mansa) and stereoselective synthesis of its two conformational isomers is challenging. We introduce a photocaged amide protection strategy: photolabile groups in monocycles reversibly modulate amide geometry, biasing macrolactamization to selectively give Pansa or Mansa. Computational studies show Mansa proceeds via a lower‐energy transition state. The method works across diverse sequences and tolerates key functional groups, confirming its robustness and broad utility. 








ABSTRACT
The fungal toxin α‐amanitin is a structurally complex bicyclic octapeptide featuring a macrolactam scaffold stabilized by a tryptathionine crossbridge critical for its conformational stability. Building on the prior development of the ansamer (Pansa/Mansa) nomenclature for an amatoxin isomer classification, the challenge of atroposelective synthesis of both isomers, the natural Pansa and non‐natural Mansa, remained. This work introduces an innovative amide bond photocaging strategy implemented on monocyclic peptide precursors, enabling the control of conformational selectivity during bicyclization to achieve the directed formation of the Pansa or Mansa atropisomer. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics simulations provide strong theoretical support for the experimentally observed atroposelectivity in Mansa formation. The methodology described could establish a paradigm for conformational control in the synthesis of bicyclic peptides, with implications for a rational conformational design across diverse peptide architectures.

title: Inside Front Cover: Operando Identification of Ni dz2 Orbital Descriptor Governing Urea Oxidation Electrocatalysis
content: Interfacial π‐π coupling between nickel phthalocyanine (NiPc) and curved carbon nanotubes enables dynamic regulation of the Ni 3d electronic structure during urea oxidation. Rather than conventional oxidation‐state evolution, electrochemical activation redistributes the Ni 3d orbitals while preserving the active Ni(II) site. The Ni 3dz2 occupancy serves as a quantitative descriptor of intrinsic activity, revealing catalyst‐support mediated frontier orbital engineering as a strategy for rational electrocatalyst design. More in the Research Article e4712106, Heng‐Liang Wu, Hui‐Lung Chen, Hao Ming Chen, and co‐workers.

title: Outside Back Cover: Hydroxyl‐Bridged Phosphorus Doping‐Induced Charge Polarization Enhancing Electron Delocalization for Efficient Photoreduction of CO2
content: OH‐bridged P atom doped carbon nitride features a unique 2N–P=OOH microstructure in heptazine units. P doping disrupts π‐π conjugation of carbon nitride. OH‐modified P doping further leads to spatial charge polarization enhancing the delocalization of electrons. Water interacts with P‐OH to enable chemical adsorption of CO2. This collectively supports the efficient CO2 photoreduction to CO. More in Research Article e3254251, Hainan Shi, Haozhi Wang, Xinwen Guo, and co‐workers.

title: Inside Front Cover: Transformation of Active Sites on Cobalt Sulfide Nanoclusters With Similar Nuclearities
content: In Communication e5734835, Nan Yan, Bin Chen, Zhikun Wu, and co‐workers present a dual‐ligand strategy to tune the dimensions and ligand distributions of atomically precise cobalt sulfide nanoclusters. Ligand habitat segregation and active‐site interconversion among cobalt, thiolate sulfur, and bare sulfur are revealed. Furthermore, the dipole‐moment direction and coordination number are identified as intrinsic spatial descriptors, offering new insights into cobalt sulfide catalysis.

title: The Crystal Structural Foundation of the “Rippled” Beta‐Sheet
content:
The rippled beta‐sheet was postulated by Pauling and Corey in 1953. Unlike with the closely related pleated beta‐sheet, it took decades for the conclusive experimental evidence for the motif to emerge. Over the past 5 years, our crystallographic work established the rippled antiparallel beta‐sheet as a structural motif with general features, capable of accommodating the majority of the canonical amino acids.








ABSTRACT
The “rippled” β‐sheet was theorized by Pauling and Corey in 1953, yet, unlike the pleated β‐sheet, remained obscure for well over half a century. From 2011 onward, the studies conducted independently by the Schneider, Nilsson and Raskatov laboratories provided the critical nucleus of biophysical data to support the viability of the rippled sheet, stimulating the ensuing x‐ray structural work. The first rippled sheet crystal structure was reported by us in 2022, 69 years after its prediction. The field has since witnessed a rapid expansion in terms of both crystal structural understanding and conceptual innovation concerning novel motif types. We have reported fifteen rippled sheet crystal structures thus far. Of the 20 canonical amino acids, our published studies have established 13 to be ripple‐genic, that is, capable of forming rippled sheets. Reported ripple‐genic systems range from tri‐ to heptapeptide in length. Among the newest advances are the mixed chirality motifs, capable of forming rippled sheets from single components, as well as conformationally locked rippled sheet macrocycles. The maturing crystal structural foundation is expected to stimulate many new and interesting applications including biomaterials, as well as molecular recognition of intrinsically disordered proteins and peptides.

content: In the Research Article e1863949, Jyh‐Chiang Jiang, Jong Sung Jin, Myong Yong Choi, and co‐workers developed CO2 laser‐engineered Ru single‐atoms on NiO regulate reaction intermediates and direct selective formate production from ethylene glycol, a key polyethylene terephthalate (PET)‐derived monomer. Advanced hybrid‐SIMS and operando spectroscopy provide molecular‐level insights into PET upcycling, offering new principles for catalyst design and sustainable circular‐carbon technologies.

title: Inside Back Cover: Neural Engineering Tailored by Molecular Motors With Self‐Reporting for Neuron Activation and Depression Treatment
content: In Research Article e2883647, Yang Tian, Limin Zhang, and co‐workers report MM‐VSD1, a light‐driven molecular motor coupled to a near‐infrared voltage reporter. It activates mechanosensitive TRPV1 channels in hippocampal neurons, evokes calcium influx and action potentials, and alleviates depression‐like behaviours in mice. By bridging mechanical manipulation with functional readouts, this work opens an avenue for mechano‐based therapeutic interventions.

title: Resurrecting Robust CYP152 Peroxygenases for Versatile Biocatalysis
content:
ASR of CYP152 peroxygenases generated reconstructed variants with a shift from hydroxylation in variants further from CYP152L1 to decarboxylation in those closer to CYP152L1. Three thermostable reconstructed variants tolerant to solvents, H2O2, extreme pH, and accepting non‐native substrates were obtained. CYP152‐AncG2 can catalyze one‐pot chemoenzymatic C─C bond coupling reactions and serve as a template for directed evolution. X‐ray structure and MD simulations of CYP152‐AncG2 indicate that its longer loops, surface salt bridges, and optimized access tunnels are key for enabling its superior features.








ABSTRACT
Cytochrome P450 CYP152s are attractive biocatalysts which catalyze decarboxylation and hydroxylation of fatty acids using H2O2 as a co‐substrate (peroxygenase activity). Contemporary CYP152s have limited stability and substrate scope. Here we characterized eight reconstructed variants of CYP152 obtained using ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR). The results showed that variants remote from Jeotgalicoccus sp. 8456 (CYP152L1) in the tree used for the ASR tended to catalyze hydroxylation, while nodes closer to CYP152L1 favored decarboxylation; this transition correlates with Q85H substitution and FG‐loop insertion alongside other structural features. Three reconstructed variants exhibit high Tm (66°C–76°C), tolerance to solvents, H2O2, extreme pH, and use non‐native substrates. CYP152‐AncG2 can catalyze one‐pot chemoenzymatic C─C bond coupling reactions to synthesize methoxy stilbene and can serve as a template for directed evolution. X‐ray structure at 1.83 Å and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations indicate that loop structures, surface salt bridges, and optimized access tunnels in CYP152‐AncG2 are key for enabling its superior features. These findings provide insights into the structural and evolutionary features of robust peroxygenase templates for expanding peroxygenase biocatalysis.

title: Structure‐Guided Design of Pepper‐Binding Fluorophores Through Hydrogen‐Bonding Engineering
content:
We develop a hydrogen‐bonding engineering strategy to optimize HBC and HBC620 fluorophores for the Pepper RNA aptamer, creating MBC and PBC620 with drastically improved affinity, cellular brightness, and photostability to support real‐time live‐cell RNA tracking.








ABSTRACT
Pepper fluorescent RNAs (FRs) enable spatiotemporal imaging of intracellular RNA with high resolution. Although spectral optimization of the HBC scaffold has extended coverage from cyan to red, systematic refinement of binding affinity, photostability, and brightness remains largely unexplored. We describe a hydrogen‐bonding strategy that strengthens fluorophore‐aptamer interactions by incorporating hydroxyl groups or polyethylene glycol (PEG) moieties into HBC derivatives. The resulting compounds, MBC and PBC620, bind Pepper over 6‐fold and 10‐fold more tightly than their parent dyes HBC and HBC620, respectively, and exhibit correspondingly higher signal‐to‐noise ratios and enhanced photostability, with 2.1‐fold and 1.5‐fold increases in cellular brightness. Molecular models reveal that improved affinity stems from optimally positioned hydrogen bonds with RNA nucleotides. MBC enables real‐time tracking of genomic loci with enhanced contrast compared to standard HBC. This work establishes structure‐guided interface engineering as a general strategy for improving fluorescent RNA systems.

title: Atmosphere‐Dependent Encapsulation and Dewetting in Au/ZnO: A Transient‐Overlayer Strategy for Maximizing Metal‐Support Interfacial Catalysis
content:
Redox‐driven SMSI dynamics in Au/ZnO drive a transient encapsulation–alloying–dewetting cycle that reconstructs the interface, yielding an expanded metal‐support interfacial perimeter. The cycled catalyst exhibits enhanced CO oxidation activity and sintering resistance relative to the fresh counterpart, demonstrating that a transient overlayer can serve as a precursor for interface‐engineered catalysis.








ABSTRACT
The strong metal–support interaction (SMSI) has traditionally been viewed as a static phenomenon that modulates catalysis through site blocking. Here, we challenge this classical view by demonstrating that SMSI in Au/ZnO is an atmosphere‐dependent dynamic process that can be harnessed to engineer catalytic interfaces. Using in situ transmission electron microscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we track the structural evolution of the Au/ZnO interface throughout redox cycles and reaction conditions. Under H2, oxygen vacancy formation triggers ZnOx encapsulation, followed by AuZn alloying at elevated temperature, which induces nanoparticle reconstruction and expands the metal‐support interfacial area. Upon exposure to O2, the alloy decomposes, and the ZnOx overlayer dewets into nanoislands, with some regions undergoing complete retraction. Under CO oxidation conditions, the fully encapsulated state is lost, yet the H2‐pretreated catalyst exhibits superior activity and stability. This enhancement arises from alloying‐induced interface reconstruction together with residual ZnO nanoislands that persist after dewetting, creating an enlarged and highly active metal–oxide interface. Our work demonstrates a transient‐overlayer strategy for catalyst design, in which a pre‐formed SMSI layer serves as a precursor that, through controlled redox cycling or reaction conditions, transforms into a high‐interface area, sintering‐resistant catalytic architecture, thereby transcending the classical encapsulation‐activity dilemma.

title: Bilayer Na‐MMT‐Intercalated Guar Gum Triboelectric Nanogenerator With Graphite‐Infused Electrodes for Machine Learning‐Assisted Neck Posture Monitoring
content:
A biodegradable guar gum‐Na‐MMT intercalated triboelectric film with graphite‐based conductive electrodes forms a self‐powered triboelectric nanogenerator. The device delivers a maximum open‐circuit voltage of 115 V, short‐circuit current of 8.5 µA, and peak power density of 11.67 µW/cm2. The distinct voltage signatures generated from flexible G‐TENG enable neck‐posture recognition, demonstrating effective AI‐assisted, sustainable wearable posture monitoring.








ABSTRACT
Prolonged screen use has fostered cervical musculoskeletal disorders, indicating the need for non‐invasive, comfortable, low‐power posture monitoring system. In this work, we developed a sustainable self‐powered triboelectric nanogenerator consisting a biodegradable guar gum‐based biopolymer for energy harvesting and neck posture monitoring. The device employing a bilayer architecture, comprises a guar gum‐bentonite triboelectric film coated with a guar gum‐graphite conductive electrode, eliminating the need for a metallic electrode. The addition of Na‐bentonite filler improves the dielectric and surface charge properties, producing a stable electrical output. As a flexible patch, the G‐TENG measures unique biomechanical voltage signals representing neck flexion and slouching posture. The analysis of these electrical signals with machine learning algorithms enables the precise classification of neck angle and sitting postures. This current study presents a strategy for green, self‐powered electronics that bridge personalized digital healthcare with sustainable biopolymers to mitigate global e‐waste.

title: Design and Navigation of Magnetic Micro/Nanorobotic Swarms in Complex Endovascular Networks: From Swarm Dynamics to Targeted Therapeutics
content:
Single magnetic micro/nanorobots face significant challenges in complex vascular environments, including weak imaging signals, limited payload capacity, and inadequate adherence at vascular bifurcations. This review addresses how programmable magnetic swarms can overcome these limitations through collective interactions, adaptive navigation, task‐specific endovascular intervention, and coordinated therapeutic functions, highlighting their potential for overcoming vascular barriers and advancing targeted biomedical applications.








ABSTRACT
The human vascular network, with its intricate geometries and diverse flow regimes, represents a formidable frontier for microrobotic navigation. While isolated microrobots frequently reach their functional ceiling due to weak signal contrast, low payload capacity, and susceptibility to hydrodynamic drag, the emergence of programmable micro/nanorobotic swarms offers a strategy to overcome these limitations in vascular intervention. By harnessing collective intelligence and programmable behavior, these swarms enhance positional stability, detectability in hard‐to‐reach circulatory environments, and versatility across endovascular tasks. This review provides a critical synthesis of magnetic actuation as an effective strategy for governing these collectives, owing to its deep‐tissue penetration and precise spatiotemporal control. An integrated design framework bridges fundamental physical principles and practical swarm‐engineering strategies with their translational potential in endovascular medicine, emphasizing relationships among collective structure, swarm dynamics, and navigation. These collective structures facilitate amplified imaging signals, high local therapeutic payloads, and task‐specific interventions, enabling robust navigation through tortuous vascular networks. By evaluating the transition from laboratory prototypes toward clinical applications, this work highlights the integrated advances required to overcome biosafety and scalability hurdles. Ultimately, programmable magnetic swarms emerge as a versatile platform with considerable potential for high‐precision, minimally invasive endovascular medicine.

title: Accelerating Molecular Ferroelectrics: From Rapid Mapping to Scalable High‐Yield Synthesis
content:
An integrated fluidic framework enables rapid crystallization screening of molecular ferroelectrics and bridges single‐crystal growth with high‐yield continuous production using pressurized CO2 as a tunable antisolvent.








ABSTRACT
Molecular ferroelectrics (MFs) represent a transformative class of functional materials, which offer mechanical flexibility, low‐density architectures, and chemical tunability. However, their development is bottlenecked by empirical, “trial‐and‐error” crystallization methods that impede both structural determination and scalable synthetic routes. Here, we present an integrated flow‐assisted crystallization screening framework that could transform the discovery and processing of MFs from an empirical approach into a quantitative, data‐driven workflow. Using the molecular ferroelectric [Co(n‐BuDABCO)Br3] (1) as a robust MF reference, we demonstrate the rapid mapping of multidimensional crystallization space. We establish a scalable framework for the accelerated synthesis, to identify conditions that yield single‐crystal‐quality XRD material within minutes. This methodology is subsequently translated to continuous‐flow synthesis in ethanol, further intensified by the introduction of CO2 as a sustainable anti‐solvent. Across the screened CO2/EtOH operating conditions, phase‐pure crystalline powders are recovered in consistently high yields up to 97%. While the high thermodynamic stability of 1 precludes the formation of new polymorphs for this system, this proof‐of‐concept highlights the viability of accessing crystallization regimes in non‐classical media, providing an adaptable strategy for the future screening and development of MFs and related multifunctional materials.

title: Super‐Paraelectric Regulation of Energy Storage Performance in Sm2O3‐Doped (Ba,Sr)TiO3 Films via Nanostructure Engineering
content:
This work proposes a Sm2O3‐doping‐induced super‐paraelectric regulation strategy to boost the energy storage performance of BaTiO3‐based films. The lead‐free, five‐element (1‐x)(Ba0.8Sr0.2)TiO3‐xSm2O3 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5) system introduces immiscible second‐phase Sm2O3 to create strong chemical and structural heterogeneity, driving the transition from normal ferroelectric to super‐paraelectric state.








ABSTRACT
This work presents a strategy for enhancing the energy storage performance in BaTiO3‐based nanocomposite films through a super‐paraelectric regulation approach enabled by Sm2O3 doping. The proposed lead‐free (1‐x)(Ba0.8Sr0.2)TiO3‐xSm2O3 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5) films contain only five elements, making them environmentally friendly and simple in composition. The incorporation of Sm2O3 as an immiscible second phase within the (Ba0.8Sr0.2)TiO3 matrix induces significant chemical and structural heterogeneity, inducing a transition from a conventional ferroelectric state to a super‐paraelectric state. In combination with an enhanced breakdown strength, this design results in an ultrahigh energy storage efficiency (η) exceeding 80%, along with a remarkable recoverable energy storage density (Ue) of 50.6 and 59.2 J/cm3 at Sm2O3 contents of x = 0.4 and 0.5. Furthermore, the films with x = 0.4 and 0.5 exhibit superior frequency (20 Hz to 5 kHz) and thermal stability (25°C–160°C), highlighting exceptional operational reliability and robustness under varying conditions. This study demonstrates that the proposed super‐paraelectric regulation strategy provides a practical pathway for designing compositionally optimized and eco‐friendly energy storage materials.

title: Engineering ApoE‐Mimetic HDL‐Like Nanoparticles for Glioblastoma‐Targeted Theranostics
content:
An ApoE‐mimetic peptide enables the stable formation of sub‐30 nm HDL‐like nanoparticles (ApoEm‐PLP) that simultaneously engage multiple lipoprotein receptors. This multivalent receptor interaction facilitates the transport of ApoEm‐PLP into brain and enhances targeted delivery of ApoEm‐PLP to glioblastoma, resulting in uniform intratumoral porphyrin deposition, improved tumor‐selective fluorescence contrast, and effective photodynamic therapy (PDT).








ABSTRACT
Glioblastoma theranostics remain limited by the tumor's blood–brain‐barrier (BBB), infiltrative growth, and heterogenous, treatment‐resistant cell populations. Here, we engineered self‐assembled high‐density lipoprotein (HDL)‐like nanoparticles functionalized with an apolipoprotein E–mimetic peptide (ApoEm), designed to recapitulate and strengthen the multireceptor‐mediated transport properties of native apolipoprotein E3 (ApoE3). Competition and receptor inhibition studies demonstrate coordinated uptake of ApoEm‐HDL nanoparticle via low‐density lipoprotein receptor, low‐density lipoprotein receptor–related protein 1, and scavenger receptor class‐B type 1, which are expressed at BBB and upregulated in glioblastoma. Incorporation of porphyrin‐lipid into the HDL‐like scaffold yielded ApoEm porphyrin–lipoprotein nanoparticles (ApoEm‐PLP) with a uniform, spherical morphology (∼30 nm). ApoEm‐PLP increased porphyrin uptake relative to ApoE3‐PLP across multiple glioblastoma cell lines (∼seven‐fold in U87 cells, ∼four‐fold in T98, and GL261‐Luc cells) and induced ∼two‐fold greater photodynamic therapy (PDT) efficacy in U87 cells. In an orthotopic U87 glioblastoma model, intravenous administration of ApoEm‐PLP achieved ∼13‐fold higher tumor porphyrin accumulation than normal brain, with homogeneous intratumoral distribution and pronounced peri‐tumoral deposition. Transcranial PDT using ApoEm‐PLP elicited widespread tumor damage. These findings establish ApoEm‐HDL‐like nanoparticles as a promising theranostic platform for uniform glioblastoma porphyrin delivery and effective phototherapy, with potential to address the infiltrative and heterogenous nature of glioblastoma.

title: Biophysics in Lipid Membranes: Advanced Experimental Platforms for Artificial Membrane Transport
content:
Artificial membrane transport systems serve as platforms for probing ion and molecular translocation across lipid bilayers. This review article cover advanced biophysical fluorescence‐ and non‐fluorescence‐based methodologies for investigating these transport processes, emphasizing their respective strengths, limitations, and applications to guide mechanistic elucidation of synthetic membrane transporters.








ABSTRACT
Artificial membrane transport systems have attracted growing interest as simplified models of biological membranes in supramolecular chemistry, chemical biology, and medicine. A wide variety of membrane‐active architectures have been realized, including artificial ion translocators, transmembrane signal transducers, cell‐penetrating peptides (CPPs), and related systems for transport across biological membranes. These systems mediate ion translocation, molecule uptake, and signaling events across a lipid bilayer, holding significant potential for applications in medicine, sensors, materials, and artificial cells. In this review article, we provide a comprehensive overview of different techniques used to evaluate the transport properties of synthetic systems across lipid bilayer membranes. The current review aims to make a collection of various established fluorescence‐ and non‐fluorescence‐based assays. This review demonstrates how carefully conducted experiments and the combination of complementary methods can ensure data reliability and deepen our understanding of the interplay among transport efficiency, selectivity, and mechanism.

title: DNA Nanotechnology for Precision Sensing and Diagnostics at the Nanoscale
content:
This work provides a comprehensive review of recent advances in DNA nanotechnology for precision sensing, as well as emerging diagnostic applications. Particular emphasis is placed on how nanoscale programmability can improve measurement resolution, enable parallel analysis of multiple molecular signals and facilitate the interpretation of biological information. Together, these developments highlight the potential of DNA nanotechnology for next‐generation precision biosensing and diagnostic platforms.








ABSTRACT
DNA nanotechnology provides a programmable framework for acquiring and processing biomolecular information with high precision. Structural DNA nanostructures enable nanoscale organization, molecular addressability and mechanical control, while dynamic DNA reaction networks support signal transduction and molecular computation. This review highlights recent advances in DNA nanotechnology for spatial, mechanical and single‐molecule sensing, as well as emerging diagnostic applications based on molecular classifiers and DNA origami‐enabled signal processing. Particular emphasis is placed on how nanoscale programmability can improve measurement resolution, enable parallel analysis of multiple molecular signals and facilitate the interpretation of biological information. These developments collectively highlight the potential of DNA nanotechnology for next‐generation precision biosensing and diagnostic platforms.
